📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In his journal entry for that day, Carter recorded his reply to Lord Carnarvon as 'Yes, it is wonderful.' The famous line comes from his 1923 book.

On November 26, 1922, in Egypt’s Valley of the Kings, Howard Carter held a candle up to a small hole in a sealed doorway and looked into the tomb of Tutankhamun for the first time.

Sources indicate that what he noted next is one of the most quoted lines in archaeology. In his published account, Carter, asked whether he could see anything, answered, “Yes, wonderful things.”.

But in the journal he kept during the excavation, Carter wrote down a different reply.

It has been revealed that carter’s handwritten journal for the first season of work on the tomb is held by the Griffith Institute at the University of Oxford, which has published a transcript online. Its entry for November 26, 1922, describes the moment step by step.

That afternoon, after clearing 9 meters (about 30 feet) of a descending passage, the team reached a second sealed doorway.

Carter made “a tiny breach in the top left hand corner to see what was beyond.” Candles were brought, he wrote, as a test for foul gases.

Carter’s patron, Lord Carnarvon, his daughter Lady Evelyn Herbert and Carter’s colleague Arthur Callender waited “in anxious expectation,” Carter wrote. “It was sometime before one could see, the hot air escaping caused the candle to flicker,” he added.

Then the room appeared, “with its strange and wonderful medley of extraordinary and beautiful objects heaped upon one another.”.

“There was naturally short suspense for those present who could not see, when Lord Carnarvon noted to me ‘Can you see anything’. I replied to him Yes, it is wonderful,” the entry reads.

It has been revealed that the more famous version appeared in 1923 in the first volume of “The Tomb of Tut.Ankh.Amen,” credited to Carter and A. C. Mace, an associate curator at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in Newly introduced York.

In the book, Carter describes seeing “strange animals, statues, and gold” and “everywhere the glint of gold.”.

He writes that he was “struck dumb with amazement,” and that when Carnarvon asked, “Can you see anything?” it was all he could do “to get out the words, ‘Yes, wonderful things.'”.

Industry observers note that the journal does not settle exactly what Carter said out loud in that passageway. But it shows that the line most people know comes from the book, not from the words Carter wrote in his journal.

Industry observers note that the journal entry goes on to list what the light revealed. Carter wrote of “two strange ebony-black effigies of a King, gold sandalled, bearing staff and mace,” gilded couches, painted caskets, alabaster vases, “a golden inlaid throne” and “a confusion of overturned parts of chariots glinting with gold.”.

His first impression, he wrote, was of “the property-room of an opera-house of a vanished civilization.”.

In a recent development, the team was not even sure it had found a royal burial. Even that afternoon, Carter wrote, the passage had seemed to support “our first conjecture that we had found a cache.”.

Then they saw a sealed doorway between two guardian statues and the name of Tutankhamun on most of the objects.

Sources indicate that “Was it a tomb or merely a cache?” Carter asked in the journal. With the evidence in front of them, he concluded, “there was little doubt that there behind was the grave of that Pharaoh.”.

The next day, Callender set up electric lights, and the group made a careful inspection of the room, which came to be called the Antechamber.

The look inside came 22 days after the first sign of the tomb. According to the Griffith Institute, Carter’s journal covers the discovery of the tomb’s stairway on November 4, 1922, and the uncovering of the first sealed doorway on November 5.

On November 4, Carter wrote, “At about 10am I discovered beneath almost the first hut attacked the first traces of the entrance of the tomb.” By sunset the next day, the workers had cleared down to the 12th step and exposed the top of a plastered, sealed doorway.

In a recent development, carter then sent a cable to Carnarvon, who was in England. “At last have made wonderful discovery in Valley a magnificent tomb with seals intact recovered same for your arrival congratulations,” it read, as copied into the journal.

More than a century later, the tomb still needs protecting. Earth.com has reported on cracks from water damage that threaten King Tut’s painted tomb and on another long-lost royal tomb that has emerged in Egypt.

According to recent reports, the information was obtained from Howard Carter’s journal for the 1922-23 excavation season, as transcribed by the Griffith Institute, University of Oxford, and from the first volume of The Tomb of Tut.Ankh.Amen by Howard Carter and A. C. Mace (1923).

Bipartisan process for picking GAO chief breaks down

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept.
  • Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.
  • It has been revealed that sources stated Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who at the moment serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

It has been revealed that sources stated Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who at the moment serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

In a recent development, senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”.

According to recent reports, the post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

The move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

According to recent reports, homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Industry observers note that paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He stated the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”.

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

Sources indicate that in 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Recent findings suggest that reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

Recent findings suggest that after Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

According to recent reports, clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

Sources indicate that “The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker stated. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”.

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

It has been revealed that over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this important position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

The Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

Sources indicate that collins remarked in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”.

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

The 8 Best Smokers to Cook Low and Slow

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • The best smokers help you achieve the sweet and savory flavor combinations that make smoked meat so tasty.
  • There isn’t just one type of smoker.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The best smokers help you achieve the sweet and savory flavor combinations that make smoked meat so tasty. Whether pulled pork, brisket, ribs, or chicken is on the menu, this type of specialized home grill brings a upcoming dimension to your backyard barbecues all year long.

There isn’t just one type of smoker. Purists prefer the iconic offset or “barrel” smoker, which reflects an array of regional barbecue traditions found in Texas, Memphis, Kansas City, and the Carolinas. In the last decade or so, increased interest in the art of barbecue has led to an expanded range of more beginner-friendly alternatives, including hardwood charcoal smokers and low-maintenance wood pellet smokers.

Industry observers note that some models have made the cooking process even easier with WiFi-enabled smart features for monitoring and adjusting internal temperature via an app on your phone. That way, you don’t have to stand by for hours as you cook.

It has been revealed that if you’re in the market for a new smoker, we have one for every setup and skill level. Continue reading for our choices of the best smokers and tips on what to consider before you buy.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve tested dozens of grills and smokers of all different shapes and sizes over the years. Tony Carrick, coauthor of this article, currently uses a Masterbuilt charcoal-fed gravity smoker and a Weber Smokey Joe at home. David Dritsas is a reviews editor at Popular Mechanics and is an amateur cook who has tested a variety of grills. Both drew on their combined experience with smokers, along with external research, to inform our recommendations.

We supplemented our own experience and criteria for smokers with extensive research into the various types that are available. We compared specifications of dozens of smokers and consulted user reviews to find trends or qualities that stand out (both positively and negatively) and might impact your ultimate choice. Our final recommendations span a range of designs and price points, and each offers solid performance, durable build quality, and great value.

Industry observers note that one of the first things you notice about the Pit Boss Navigator 1600M is how well-constructed it is. The metal frame is sturdy, the hardware is strong, and the main section is well-insulated, including a heavy hood that is lined all the way around the edges by a fireproof, padded seal that keeps the heat in. (The Navigator performed very well in that regard.).

In a recent development, it has a large hopper that holds up to 30 pounds of pellets, and the controls are easy to understand. There’s WiFi on board, and we experienced a one-time concern where the app disconnected and would not reconnect, but it otherwise worked well, and navigation was intuitive. The Navigator also has two wired thermometer probes, for which you can set temperature alerts, so you know when your meats are ready.

For our main cooking test, we smoked a flat iron steak, as well as a mix of garlic-marinated zucchini, onions, and red peppers (that was enclosed in aluminum foil, open at the top). We were impressed with how rapidly the grill heated up and how efficiently it maintained the temperature (even as we grilled in cold weather).

In a recent development, the only feature we did not find exceptional was the flame broil setting, which allows you to expose food to the flames of the burner cup directly. While it technically works, the cooking area of this feature is only roughly 3 inches in diameter, so it’s not very effective for large pieces of meat or more than one burger. But that complaint is a minor one.

Full Pit Boss Navigator 1600M Review.

Industry observers note that you don’t have to spend a lot of money to get proficient at smoking food, and Oklahoma Joe’s Laredo Deluxe proves that point. It’s a very basic charcoal barrel-shaped model that requires you to stay near and mind the coals to maintain the temperature, but it offers a few nice extra features to help you do it.

The biggest is the three-position charcoal tray. Set it high to sear meat while grilling or set it low to help keep temperatures down around 250 degrees Fahrenheit when smoking low and slow. Of course, airflow is integral to smoking, and there are three control options here, including a side vent, a chimney, and a large front door that you can also open to gain access to the coals for adjustment without having to remove the cooking grates. We used it several times to spread out the charcoal when things were getting a bit too hot.

Recent findings suggest that there’s also a built-in thermometer that’s easy to read, even from a short distance, two side tables, and a lower shelf. All noted and done, even if you don’t use it as a smoker, we think this makes for a fantastic charcoal grill with plenty of cooking area (940 square inches) to make a ton of burgers for your next barbecue party.

In a recent development, the Laredo Deluxe is not as solidly constructed as some of the other selections on our list, but that’s to be expected for a grill that’s usually on sale for under $300. We smoked a delicious brisket with ease during our tests, and we’d happily do so again.

Full Oklahoma Joe’s Laredo Deluxe Grill and Smoker Review.

Recent findings suggest that masterbuilt’s Gravity Series 800 gives you unique flavor from hardwood charcoal smoke in your barbecue without dealing with all the fuss of micromanaging your smoker. It pairs a large gravity-fed hopper for hardwood charcoal with a digital thermostat that controls the internal temperature. The hopper keeps your cooking fire fed, while an internal fan system regulates temperature to maintain consistency. Just load it up, light it, and let it cook for hours with minimal maintenance.

Industry observers note that as with our top pick, the Gravity Series 800 features wireless-enabled smart controls, which allow you to monitor the temperature from your phone. It also includes a digital meat probe.

With 800 square inches of cooking surface, you’re getting a lot of space here. There’s plenty of room for ribs, whole chickens, and pork butts. But at nearly five feet wide, the Masterbuilt 800 is a massive boy—possibly too big for some decks and patios. That noted, it also functions as a standard charcoal grill and a flat-top griddle, so you could ditch your standard grill to make space for it.

This Woodridge Pro is a midrange model in Traeger’s line of pellet smokers, featuring some of the technology found in its higher-end models but at a lower price. When we unboxed the grill, we were impressed by how easy it was to put together, despite the large number of loose parts. Traeger’s assembly guide was one of the best we’ve seen, with clear directions and marked boxes with icons that corresponded to the instructions.

According to recent reports, some construction elements, such as light plastic wheels and thin grill grates, seemed lacking, and there’s no seal around the interior of the hood (which helps with heat retention). Once together, however, this grill is sturdy and not at all difficult to move around. We really appreciate that the top of the pellet hopper serves as an extra shelf, which is handy and something you don’t always get with other grills. There’s also a special pellet sensor that lets you know if pellets are running low.

Sources indicate that the Woodridge Pro is extremely straightforward to operate. The rather retro display with large block numbers is readable from a distance, and basic temperature control is quick to adjust and set with a large push-button dial. You can also set a timer, check probe temperature, and with the press of a button, add extra smoky flavor for slow cooks under 225 degrees Fahrenheit. One thing we really liked was a motion graphic that demonstrates whether the grill is heating up or lowering the temperature. During our tests, it was helpful to have that feature as a reminder as we multitasked. Wireless control is available with WiFi and Bluetooth, and the app, named WiFire, is easy to use.

The food we made turned out delicious, whether slow-cooked for a deeper smoky flavor or grilled at a higher temperature for just a hint. We used both the included wired probe to monitor temperature, as well as a Meater thermometer, and found some slight discrepancies between the grill’s temperature setting and the ambient temperature on the Meater. We found ourselves pushing the temperature up a few degrees to get it where we wanted it to be. This didn’t mar the experience too greatly, however. The Woodridge Pro is a reliable pellet grill that’s fun to use and a worthy addition to any back patio.

Full Traeger Woodridge Pro Review.

Recent findings suggest that in many ways, the 18-Inch Smokey Mountain from Weber is a standard water smoker (a 14-inch model is also available). Like similar models, it has a bottom rack and retaining ring for the charcoal, a large bowl for water, and two racks for smoking food. But it stands out because it’s made from heavier porcelain-enameled steel, which helps retain heat and maintain a consistent temperature, as well as a heat shield on the bottom to protect your deck or lawn. It also comes with a cover.

Recent findings suggest that when we first fired it up to season the smoker, we took the opportunity to get familiar with how to use the three air vents around the bottom, as well as the top vent, to help hold a desired temperature. To help you gauge this, there’s a thermometer in the lid that shows a highlighted smoking zone from 200 to 275 degrees Fahrenheit, and we found it was relatively easy to keep it in that range.

According to recent reports, we put this to the real-world test when smoking some beef jerky. To do this, we wanted to keep the temperature on the lower side at around 200 degrees Fahrenheit. This proved a little challenging; the temperature kept creeping up, so we watched it closely and adjusted the vents as needed. In the end, the jerky smoked a bit faster than we intended. In hindsight, we used a little too much charcoal, which generated more heat than we needed. While this was our mistake, it shows just how well this smoker can retain heat.

Recent findings suggest that when smoking a smaller-sized brisket, we more successfully managed the temperature and were able to hold close to 225 degrees Fahrenheit for the 5 hours it took to smoke it. One thing we really appreciated during longer smoking sessions was the large door, which made it easy to add fuel and wood chips. The Smokey Mountain is a basic smoker that will require a little experience to use effectively, but will ultimately be worth the time and produce great results. — tested by Bradley Ford.

According to recent reports, though they are frowned upon by traditionalists, electric smokers like this one from East Oak are the quickest way for new barbecuers to enter the world of smoking. Its digital controls make it easy to maintain specific temperatures, and the combination of a side wood chip loader and glass door means you can check on your cook without opening the door, which could impact your cooking temperature.

The 725-square-inch cooking surface gives you plenty of room to experiment with various types of food in a single session, but the smoker itself is quite slim, measuring nearly 19 inches wide and 18 inches deep, so it won’t take up a lot of space on your deck or patio. Bottom line: This is a straightforward and, above all, convenient way to try smoking barbecue at home.

If a grill could be a pop-culture icon, the Major Green Egg is it. The brand has a whole group of fans—known as Eggheads—who gather at grilling events called EGGfests held all across the country. And it’s not just home enthusiasts. According to the company, nearly 1,800 restaurants use this extremely popular kamado grill. Its excellent heat retention and temperature range, enabled by its shape and porcelain-coated ceramic enclosures, make them an instant upgrade over your average gas or charcoal grill.

That thick ceramic body is also very effective at retaining heat, making it very effective for cooking low and slow. Just add some smoking wood, and you can smoke a brisket overnight. This grill can get as hot as 750 degrees Fahrenheit when you’re grilling, but smokers will want to maintain a stable 225 to 300 degrees using the air vents at the top and the bottom of the egg. And it’s large enough to feed a crowd—we’re talking about smoking a 20-pound turkey for Thanksgiving.

It has been revealed that this small electric smoker from GE lets you take your smoking indoors. It uses two heat sources—one to cook food and the other to burn pellets—along with a filtration device to prevent the smoke from filling your kitchen. Its modest 293 square inches of cooking surface is enough to smoke three half racks of ribs or a small pork butt.

There’s a bevy of controls for setting smoke levels and adjusting temperatures. There are also preset food settings, including brisket, ribs, pork butt, and chicken wings. Built-in probes and WiFi connectivity let you monitor meat temperatures remotely, and this smoker is compatible with voice controls via Amazon Alexa and Google Home.

Full GE Indoor Electric Smoker Review.

According to recent reports, traditional offset or “barrel” smokers feature two parts: A large main cooking chamber for your food and a smaller cook box for the fuel. The wood or charcoal burns, heating the main chamber and filling it with smoke, which slowly cooks the meat with indirect heat and infuses it with smoky flavor. Offset smokers, like the Royal Gourmet model we recommend as our Best Value pick, are beloved by barbecue aficionados, but are also the most challenging to use. Learning how to control the temperature in an offset smoker takes practice.

Industry observers note that vertical or “cabinet” smokers have a tall, closet-like design with a single door on the front and three to five racks for food inside. The heat source sits in the base, allowing the heat and smoke to waft upward and fill the space. Going high instead of wide makes a vertical smoker more compact, so it’s a good option if you don’t have much room on your patio. That said, the narrow profile may limit your ability to cook large pieces of meat, such as a full rack of ribs.

Like vertical smokers, the pill-shaped bullet smoker has a fuel area at the bottom with the main cooking chamber above. Vents on the bottom and top of the smoker allow you to control the temperature inside the chamber, and a water pan sits just below the cook area to keep food moist. Bullet smokers are compact, however, and some models are stacked so tightly that you may have trouble accessing the food on the middle racks mid-cook.

Industry observers note that most pellet smokers, including the Traeger Ironwood 885, look more like a grill than a smoker, with a wide cook box and a clamshell lid that opens up to reveal a broad cooking surface. To generate smoke and heat, an electric auger feeds small hardwood pellets from a hopper on the back or side into a fire inside the cook box. The auger automatically adds fuel to the fire based on the temperature you dial in on the smoker’s digital thermostat, so you don’t need to babysit the smoker to maintain the proper temperature. However, they require a power source and tend to be the most expensive.

According to recent reports, kamado grills, like the famous Significant Green Egg, are hybrid grill-smokers. These large, acorn-shaped ceramic cook boxes can maintain low temperatures for many hours or build up scorching heat with temperatures that eclipse 800 degrees. It’s an incredibly versatile option, which has made it a gateway device for new barbecuers.

Smokers can use a variety of fuel types, including hardwood, charcoal, gas, electricity, or wood pellets. Hardwood and charcoal are the fuels of choice for smoking purists. This combination creates a lot of smoke, maximizing that flavor. Maintaining a consistent low temperature takes time to learn, though, and it makes more of a mess with leftover ash.

Electric and gas smokers are convenient because they require little to no maintenance, but they don’t inherently produce smoke. Instead, they rely on wood chip trays that aren’t as effective as wood, charcoal, or pellets at instilling flavor into food. However, they still can produce decent results.

Sources indicate that pellet smokers use compressed wood pellets that generate real smoke for instilling flavor into food, while minimizing maintenance with automatic temperature regulation. Pellet grills offer excellent heat retention and temperature control, but don’t need as much constant attention as charcoal or wood grills.

In a recent development, smoking meat can take eight hours or more, depending on the cut, so you’ll probably want to cook as much as you can in one session. It’s notable to look for a smoker with an efficient interior design that has space for everything you want to cook. The average cooking surface size for a smoker is around 550 square inches, which is enough to fit five full racks of ribs, four whole chickens, or five pork butts. That noted, I’ve seen cooking surfaces range in size from 250 square inches to more than 800.

Recent findings suggest that some modern smokers can connect to your smartphone via Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, allowing you to track their internal temperature, change temperature settings, and monitor meat probes remotely through an app. They can also send you alerts if the smoker’s internal temperature rises or falls, the food reaches a target temperature, or if it’s low on fuel, allowing you to keep tabs on your smoker without having to hover over it.

What’s the best temperature for smoking meat?

It has been revealed that with a smoker, you want to keep the temperature low and cook for a long time. Depending on what you’re cooking, I’d recommend maintaining your heat between 190 and 225 degrees. In that range, you will cook your meat slowly enough to make it incredibly tender and infuse it with smoky flavor.

How long does it take to smoke meat?

In a recent development, it depends on what you’re cooking. Smoking a rack of ribs typically takes between four and five hours, but a pork butt may need 8 to 10 hours. Brisket is well-known for needing an especially long smoke—around 12 to 18 hours.

Can I use my gas grill as a smoker?

Technically, yes. You can add a smoker box to a gas grill, which holds wood chips to generate smoke. So long as you keep the top of the grill closed, that’s a smoker. Make sure to set up the grill so that the food is not sitting directly above the heat source, and set the burners so that the grill only heats to a maximum of 225 degrees with the lid closed.

In a recent development, that stated, it’s far from ideal. It’s more difficult to maintain the consistently low temperatures needed for smoking with a gas grill than it is with a dedicated smoker. On top of that, flames from a gas grill will not impart the same distinctive taste as a proper smoker burning charcoal or hardwood. (Purists don’t even like gas as a fuel for dedicated smokers.).

He’s tested and written about everything from home security systems to power tools to gas grills. He has over 25 years of experience writing about and reviewing consumer electronics, kitchen appliances, DIY products, outdoor gear, and more. Latest Update: Cougars battle deep snow and freezing weather every winter, but nature is not what kills most of them

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1162 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People, not weather, caused most deaths among tracked cougars.
  • Sources indicate that you might expect deep snow and bitter cold to be the biggest threat to a wild animal in winter.
  • Industry observers note that of 80 cougars fitted with tracking collars, 37 died, and people caused 29 of those deaths.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People, not weather, caused most deaths among tracked cougars. The hunting season, roads, and human houses each play a role.

Sources indicate that you might expect deep snow and bitter cold to be the biggest threat to a wild animal in winter. Yet when researchers tracked cougars across five winters in the foothills of Alberta’s Rocky Mountains, they found the weather was not what killed them. People were.

Industry observers note that of 80 cougars fitted with tracking collars, 37 died, and people caused 29 of those deaths. Nearly all of them came between November and March, and Alberta’s cougar hunting season falls inside those months.

Where a cougar spent its time mattered too. Cats that stayed close to houses and unpaved roads died at higher rates than cats that kept away from them.

Carter Littlefair and Andrew Derocher of the University of Alberta’s Department of Biological Sciences led the study. Their co-authors, Paul Frame and Mark Edwards, work at Alberta Environment and Protected Areas, the province’s environment ministry.

Sources indicate that between 2016 and 2021, the team used hounds to tree cougars in the country south of Whitecourt and north of Sundre. They then darted each cat and fitted a GPS collar. The collars reported a location every seven hours.

According to recent reports, the 80 cats were followed for a little over a year each, on average. When a collar signaled a death, crew reached the site within three days to work out what had happened.

Hunters killed 16 of the 37 that died. Another eight died in traps set for other animals, and two were hit by vehicles. Three more were killed as problem animals or by landowners with permission.

Wolves killed three adult females, two of them with kittens still depending on them. Seven deaths in all were natural, and one could not be explained. The cats share this country with wolves, black bears, and grizzlies, and their main prey is white-tailed deer.

In an average year, a collared cougar had a 60 percent chance of living through the next 12 months. That figure hides a split between the seasons.

Industry observers note that from April through October, 96 percent of the cats survived. From November through March, only 62 percent did.

Sources indicate that cougar hunting in the study area opens on December 1 and closes at the end of February, or earlier once an area’s quota is filled. Hunters there use hounds to follow a track and tree the cat. Of the 37 cougars that died, 33 died in the cold months.

Since 2019, the province has set each area’s hunting quota at roughly 14 to 16 percent of the cougars it estimates live there.

In an interview with Earth.com, Littlefair said that lowering harvest limits would have the greatest direct effect on survival, since hunting caused the majority of the deaths the team documented.

Alberta’s system lets each management area’s limits be adjusted every year, separately for males and females, and the findings can help inform how they are set, Littlefair said.

According to recent reports, the team then asked which parts of the landscape went with dying. Rugged terrain and forest edges, which the team expected to make a cat easier to spot or reach, made no difference to survival.

Industry observers note that what mattered was access. A cougar within about 490 feet (150 meters) of a house faced a much higher risk of death than one farther away. So did a cougar within about 165 feet (50 meters) of an unpaved road.

The authors suggested a reason: a hound hunt begins with a track rather than a sighting, and hunters find those tracks along roads and cutlines before the chase starts.

“Mortality risk increased with proximity to residences and secondary roads, indicating that cougars occupying accessible areas were more vulnerable to harvest,” they wrote.

Cats that crossed cutlines, pipelines, power lines, and seismic lines more often as they traveled were also more likely to die. Logging and oil and gas work have left this part of Alberta with a dense network of unpaved roads.

Littlefair said that reducing the density of roads and other human-made disturbances across the landscape could also help lower that risk.

Familiar ground did not seem to protect them either. Of 15 cougars whose previous year’s range could be mapped, 12 died inside it.

Alberta’s rules are built to steer hunters toward males. Quotas allow more males than females, and a female with kittens is off limits. Hunters using hounds also tend to select large males.

Sources indicate that so the team expected males to die more frequently, as they do in hunted populations elsewhere. They didn’t find that and Littlefair told Earth.com it was one of the more surprising results.

Other studies with similarly female-heavy samples have still found hunters taking more males. In this study, however, hunters killed nine females and seven males, and the team could not detect any difference in survival between the sexes.

Industry observers note that hunting did make up a bigger share of male deaths, with 64 percent in comparison to 35 percent for females. But with only 24 males in the study, that difference could have come up by chance.

Mothers were at no extra risk the team could detect: it found 18 litters, and females with kittens survived at the same rate as females without them.

Hunting’s 43 percent share of the deaths is smaller than the 62 to 75 percent reported in some other hunted cougar populations. Provincial records also show human-caused cougar deaths have fallen since a peak in 2015.

“One important distinction is that high mortality does not necessarily indicate an unsustainable population,” Littlefair noted.

Judging that would require counts that the study did not make, of the cougars there, their kittens, and the young that reach adulthood.

The study did not measure how many hunters were out or how hard they hunted, so it can’t separate a road from the people driving on it.

The authors treat a cat’s use of roads and houses as a stand-in for its chances of meeting a hunter, not as a danger in itself.

A second gap is the number of males. With 56 females and 24 males collared, the study can say less about males.

“It would certainly be interesting to repeat the study with a more balanced sample of males and females to see whether this pattern persists,” Littlefair said.

For now, the finding covers one stretch of Alberta, where a cougar’s odds of surviving the winter depend on how close it lives to a house or an unpaved road.

Littlefair and his team believe that managers should weigh that pattern of access when they judge how much hunting a population can absorb, and where it falls.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS One.

#157506. Komodo dragons have a thin layer of iron on their teeth that keeps them razor-sharp for tearing apart prey

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (773 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Komodo dragons have a thin layer of iron on their teeth that keeps them razor-sharp for tearing apart prey

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers discovered that Komodo dragons coat the serrated edges of their teeth in iron, staining them orange and keeping them razor-sharp for ripping apart prey.
  • Look closely at a Komodo dragon’s teeth, and you will notice an orange tint along the cutting edges.
  • In a 2024 study, researchers found a thin, iron-rich coating along the tips and serrated edges, concluding that it helps keep the teeth sharp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers discovered that Komodo dragons coat the serrated edges of their teeth in iron, staining them orange and keeping them razor-sharp for ripping apart prey.

Look closely at a Komodo dragon’s teeth, and you will notice an orange tint along the cutting edges. It is not a stain from feeding. Even teeth that have not yet pushed through the gums are just as orange.

The color actually comes from iron. In a 2024 study, researchers found a thin, iron-rich coating along the tips and serrated edges, concluding that it helps keep the teeth sharp.

Scientists had never seen anything like it in a meat-eating reptile before.

“Komodo dragons have curved, serrated teeth to rip and tear their prey just like those of meat-eating dinosaurs,” mentioned Aaron LeBlanc of King’s College London, the study’s lead author.

LeBlanc’s team looked for the same coating on fossil dinosaur teeth and saw no evidence of it. But fossilization may be the reason.

Komodo dragons are the largest predatory lizards alive, and scientists have studied their teeth before. One detail had still been overlooked.

According to recent reports, leBlanc’s team examined teeth from skeletons and from specimens preserved in fluid. Every unworn tooth tip and serration was orange.

Serrations are the small points along a cutting edge, like the ones on a steak knife.

The rest of each tooth looked white. The enamel there is transparent, so the white comes from the layer underneath, called dentin.

According to recent reports, the enamel on a Komodo dragon’s serrations and tooth tips is about 0.0008 inches (20 micrometers) thick. That’s roughly one-fifth the thickness of a sheet of printer paper.

The team found iron in the outermost layer of that enamel with every method it used. At its thickest, the iron-rich layer makes up about a tenth of the enamel’s thickness.

In a recent development, one of those methods was X-ray mapping at a type of particle accelerator called a synchrotron. Those maps showed the iron concentrated along the serrations.

With another method, the team found more oxygen where the iron was concentrated. The authors took that as a sign the coating is an iron oxide. Rust is made of iron oxides too.

How hard is the coating? On a Komodo dragon tooth, LeBlanc’s team found that difficult to test reliably, because the coating is so thin.

It has been revealed that so the team turned to a tooth shed by an American alligator at a British zoo. That tooth had iron-rich enamel thick enough to test.

Sources indicate that to test it, the team pressed a fine tip into the enamel of that one tooth 74 times. The iron-rich enamel was slightly harder than the enamel beneath it, by about 9%.

Like the team’s electron microscope and X-ray experiments, the hardness tests were each run once, on individual teeth.

Recent findings suggest that iron may make the outer enamel along a cutting edge more resistant to wear. For the Komodo dragon, that’s less certain. Its iron-rich layer is much thinner than the alligator’s.

Still, worn Komodo dragon teeth hint that the coating protects the serrations. Enamel can flake off most of a worn tooth and expose the dentin. On the serrations, the enamel appears to wear down gradually instead.

According to recent reports, komodo dragons replace their teeth rapidly. So the thin coating must be enough to keep each tooth sharp until a fresh one takes its place, the authors wrote.

Meat-eating dinosaurs had serrated teeth with thin enamel, just as Komodo dragons do.

The team also tested teeth shed by crocodiles and their relatives living in zoos. All four species, the American alligator among them, had an iron-rich outer layer of enamel.

Recent findings suggest that so the team looked for iron in fossil teeth from tyrannosaurs and from the family that includes Velociraptor. Every technique gave the same result. The team saw no consistent sign of extra iron in the enamel on the serrations.

LeBlanc’s team gave two possible explanations. Either fossilization masks the iron, or these dinosaurs didn’t normally concentrate it along their serrations. For now, the fossils can’t show which explanation is right.

“With further analysis of the Komodo teeth we may be able to find other markers in the iron coating that aren’t changed during fossilization,” LeBlanc noted.

“With markers like that we would know with certainty whether dinosaurs also had iron-coated teeth and have a greater understanding of these ferocious predators.”.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution.

An El Niño amped by climate change has California bracing for the worst

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2213 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • In parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready.
  • What is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready. The state has strategically stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators. Debris has been fished out to clear storm drains, seepage blankets shore up aging levees and dams, and wire mesh cages hold back precariously placed boulders.

What is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves. The fury of this year’s El Niño is being unleashed around the globe as well, from inundating Florida with floods to exacerbating drought in the Amazon. And much more is still to come, forecasts show, with the peak of the climate phenomenon expected to arrive between November 2026 and January 2027.

According to recent reports, californians know all too well the threat. El Niño has historically brought relentless rainfall to the state, flooding cities and triggering landslides.

State officials learned a lot about preparedness and emergency water management from previous El Niños — particularly the strong event that spanned the winter of 1997–1998. But this year’s event is likely to be even more challenging, a “Super” El Niño superimposed on the backdrop of global climate change.

Climate change has made water management in California more complicated than it was just 30 years ago — as it has elsewhere around the world, says environmental scientist Letitia Grenier, the director of water policy at the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank based in San Francisco.

Recent findings suggest that in 1997, California’s overall climate was much drier; El Niño brought a massive, long rainy season that spanned the state, Grenier says. But now, “it’s just so humid. The air is warmer, so it can hold more water.”.

Industry observers note that that waterlogged atmosphere means that even without El Niño, there’s been less of a distinct rainy season in California, and more rapid flip-flop between intense episodes of rain dumped on the ground followed by periods of heat and dryness. “It’s these strange, erratic patterns that we’ve never seen before,” she claims. And the state is bracing for how the Super El Niño will clash with this latest climate normal.

1997 was the year that the term “El Niño” shot to global fame. It was the most powerful El Niño in recorded history, and the first to be scientifically monitored in real time, continuously tracked by satellites and breathlessly reported on by news outlets. El Niño’s rise to household name status was even cemented in pop culture by an appearance on Saturday Night Live, in a classic sketch by comedian Chris Farley.

Recent findings suggest that but the event was no laughing matter. It caused global devastation during its brief reign. El Niño events form as westward-blowing trade winds over the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean weaken, allowing warm water to accumulate at the surface. Those waters can then release massive amounts of heat to the atmosphere, altering the position of the Pacific jet stream and helping to disrupt global weather patterns.

In 1997–1998, global temperatures spiked by 1.5 degrees Celsius on average. Along with the torrential rains in California, the event brought brutal drought to Southeast Asia and deadly summer floods to central Europe and Peru. Record-breaking floods also hit East Africa, which in turn triggered a surge in mosquito-borne Rift Valley fever. The oceans were so warm that 16 percent of the world’s reefs died.

In all, the El Niño–related weather extremes were linked to more than 22,000 fatalities around the world, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.

Recent findings suggest that not every El Niño is equally intense, or impacts weather in quite the same way. “There’s a lot of variability event to event,” notes Washington, D.C.–based climate scientist Tom Di Liberto, of the nonprofit climate news organization Climate Central.

Industry observers note that but there is a general overall pattern to how El Niño tends to affect weather around the planet, Di Liberto states. For example, there tend to be more tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean, and fewer in the Atlantic — a pattern also observed in 2026.

In a recent development, el Niño also tends to flatten and accelerate the Pacific jet stream, shifting its flow southward, says Mike Anderson, California’s state climatologist for the Department of Water Resources, who is based in Sacramento. And that has historically meant that a conveyor belt of back-to-back moisture-loaded storms is set on a collision course with the U.S. West Coast.

In a recent development, the El Niño rapidly strengthened during the summer of 2026. As westerly trade winds weakened, warm waters accumulated in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, raising both ocean temperatures and the sea level height (shown in this animation). Red and white colors indicate the highest sea level. Beginning in April and intensifying through November, the El Niño event generated Kelvin waves, massive swells that sweep eastward along the equator toward the Americas.

The 1997–1998 El Niño revealed just how devastating that pattern could be in California.

As much as 30 centimeters inundated parts of the state during the month of February 1998 alone. Storm winds and high surf pounded the coast, while rivers swelled and overtopped their banks. Flooding from the “Groundhog Day Storm” destroyed some 1,700 homes in Bay Area cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park. On February 6 near Rio Nido, about 100 kilometers from San Francisco, a forested hillside suddenly crumbled, sending a wall of mud rushing down the mountain. It destroyed about 30 homes.

Landslides also threatened homes and lives in Southern California.

Industry observers note that on February 23, then 25-year-old Jenifer Segraves and her fiancé Glenn Flook were living in an apartment on Laguna Canyon Road, in the city of Laguna Beach. The heavy rains had saturated the neighborhood’s steep hillsides, making the terrain unstable.

Sources indicate that “We lived up against a hill in the canyon, so there were stairs up to our apartment,” Segraves says now. “They became like a waterfall. I remember my fiancé carrying me up the stairs because there was so much water.” Segraves called her father, Gary Segraves, in a panic, asking for help. Then, the slope behind the building failed, the apartment flooded and she and Flook fled into the rushing mud.

It has been revealed that “We were strong enough to get out, but we were waist-high in mud,” Segraves mentioned. “[My dad] almost drowned getting to us.” All three took shelter at a neighbor’s house, where they showered and hunkered down to wait out the rain.

Around midnight on February 24, the second mudslide arrived.

The neighbor’s “whole house went down,” Segraves claims. She escaped through a second-floor window, but her fiancé fell through the floor and was knocked out. He didn’t make it out.

Gary Segraves, meanwhile, was swept down the hillside and landed in a pile of rubble against a rocky cliff. Battered and missing his glasses, he looked around and saw what looked like a doll.

Industry observers note that he reached for the little form — and discovered that it was a baby, very cold but alive. Somehow, the 9-month-old had survived being swept out of her crib from a nearby home. The little girl “wouldn’t have survived if he hadn’t picked her up,” Segraves indicates.

Industry observers note that the havoc wreaked across California by the event 30 years ago cast a stark light on the desperate need to expand waterways, maintain infrastructure and coordinate emergency services, Grenier indicates. “An engineering system can only work as well as its capacity.”.

Recent findings suggest that much of the state’s infrastructure is deteriorating. An October 13 report by the California state auditor noted that the condition of dams and levees across the state “remains a high-risk glitch,” with some 57 dams in the state in poor or unsatisfactory condition. “Poorly maintained dams and levees continue to pose a risk to public safety,” the report remarked.

California’s water management system was also originally designed specifically to simply shunt excess water away from residential areas, rather than try to capture the water or help it infiltrate into aquifers, Grenier says. But that system worked for a different climate, one that wasn’t so prone to “weather whiplash” — wild, sudden swings between extremely wet and extremely dry conditions.

Alongside punishing, drenching back-to-back storms called atmospheric rivers, the state has also experienced frequent episodes of drought, including two recent severe events, one lasting from 2012 to 2016 and another from 2021 to 2025.

In a recent development, those years of drought, dwindling snow and pumping too much water from aquifers have dramatically depleted the state’s subsurface water stores. And the heavy rains don’t necessarily help; the torrents of water mostly run off across the surface instead of infiltrating soils to reach the underground aquifer.

In a recent development, such hydroclimate whiplash isn’t unique to California by any means. It’s a global problem, and it’s becoming more common. A small increase in air temperatures can give a significant boost to the atmosphere’s capacity to hold water vapor, increasing that capacity by about 7 percent for every 1 degree C of temperature increase. All of that water vapor has contributed to an increase in extreme precipitation events around the globe since the mid-20th century.

Precipitation is just half of the problem. Rising air temperatures also make the air “thirstier,” causing it to draw even more moisture out of vegetation, soil and surface bodies of water during drier periods — which makes the land more vulnerable to severe drought and wildfire.

According to recent reports, it’s now clear that these hydrodynamic shifts have been increasing the frequency of weather whiplash events around the world over the last 75 years or so, scientists reported in 2025. And that whiplash is likely to increase as the world warms more.

Months before reaching peak intensity, the 2026–2027 Super El Niño has begun making its presence known. The Amazon is suffering under intense heat and drought, priming the region for wildfires and pushing the forest closer to a worrisome possible fate: a transition from tropical forest to savanna grasslands. Fires have also begun blazing across Southeast Asia, while heavy rains began inundating the Horn of Africa in October. Arriving on the heels of severe drought, that one-two punch could devastate the region’s crops and pasturelands.

Industry observers note that in California, the first harbingers of the arrival of the Super El Niño appeared in early September. Heavy surf pounded the coastline. Regions from San Francisco to Los Angeles saw record high tides by late October that flooded city streets and battered coastlines and seawalls, even as the skies remained clear.

The waves were amped up by an unfortunate trifecta: higher sea levels due to climate change; a lunar cycle that exerted its maximum pull on the tides; and an El Niño–linked phenomenon called Kelvin waves.

Kelvin waves are massive, slow-moving swells of warm ocean water, part of the complicated interplay between wind and water that produces the El Niño Southern Oscillation, the overall weather pattern that includes El Niño and counterpart La Niña events, says Josh Willis, an oceanographer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif.

Sources indicate that as prevailing west-blowing winds weaken over the tropical eastern Pacific, Willis says, water normally pushed west by the winds instead sloshes back eastward. Kelvin waves have historically given a boost to sea levels along the U.S. West Coast of as much as 30 centimeters. This year, that impact could be larger, researchers reported September 30 in a preprint study posted on EarthArXiv.org. Computer model simulations suggest that the risk of the risk of extreme sea levels could be 10 times higher during this El Niño year than during previous events, for coastlines from Alaska all the way to Chile.

Then, by late October, the Santa Ana winds arrived: Hot, dry gusts blowing down the mountains toward the coast, fanning wildfires in Southern California. The fires scarred the landscape, denuding it of vegetation, roots that helped stabilize and fortify the soil. Such loosened soil is more likely to become mobilized into a debris flow during heavy rains.

Those rains are now on the way. By mid-November, researchers began tracking storms headed for California. The peak of El Niño is expected to arrive by late November or early December and persist through February or March.

In a recent development, segraves, after surviving nearly 30 years ago, indicates she is aware that another El Niño is coming. But she hasn’t been following the news closely. She’s placed herself on a news diet since her ordeal. She refused to speak to media for years, or even read the coverage about her own story.

Industry observers note that “Everyone wanted to talk to me and I just wanted to be left alone,” she indicates. Staying away from the news “freed me from all that. It changed my view on life. I take each day as it comes.”.

It has been revealed that but, she adds, one lesson has stayed with her. “I swore I would never live on a cliff again.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.
  • The Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

The Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

“The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition says.

Trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

According to recent reports, immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

Sources indicate that the D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a newly introduced removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”.

Industry observers note that last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

The case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that grand Teton hunters must use non-lead ammunition, carry bear spray and turn in every elk head for chronic wasting disease testing.
  • In Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming, a small number of licensed hunters are allowed to take elk inside the park until December 6.
  • The annual elk reduction program runs from November 14 through December 6, according to the National Park Service.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that grand Teton hunters must use non-lead ammunition, carry bear spray and turn in every elk head for chronic wasting disease testing. Visitors should wear bright colors.

In Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming, a small number of licensed hunters are allowed to take elk inside the park until December 6.

The annual elk reduction program runs from November 14 through December 6, according to the National Park Service.

It is authorized under the park’s 1950 enabling legislation and managed jointly by the Park Service and the Wyoming Game and Fish Department.

This year, only 40 permits are authorized, and hunters may take only cows and calves.

After reviewing available biological data, the Park Service and Wyoming Game and Fish determined that the program is necessary “to maintain the herd at its population objective and achieve desired elk distribution,” according to the Park Service.

It has been revealed that the program uses Wyoming-licensed hunters with limited-quota permits to harvest elk in designated areas. The Park Service calls it “an important management tool with requirements that distinguish it from traditional elk hunting programs.”.

Participants must carry a state license for Elk Hunt Area 75, a conservation stamp, an elk special management permit, a 2026 park elk reduction program permit and a hunter education card, regardless of age.

They must use non-lead ammunition and wear fluorescent orange or pink clothing. They also have to carry bear spray that is immediately accessible, in a non-expired can of at least 7.9 ounces.

Archery equipment, handguns, non-centerfire rifles and artificial elk calls are prohibited, the Park Service claims.

Sources indicate that only Area 75 is open for the program this year. It lies mostly east of U.S. Highway 89, according to the park.

Within Area 75, the Antelope Flats portion and the Snake River bottom between Deadman’s Bar and Ditch Creek are closed throughout the season.

Area 79 is closed to the program this season “to limit harvest pressure on northern migratory and resident elk,” the park indicates.

To support surveillance for chronic wasting disease, known as CWD, participants must turn in the head of every elk harvested in the park at the designated drop-off location in Moose.

Park staff collect lymph nodes and send them to the Wyoming Game and Fish Wildlife Health Lab for testing, and hunters can check their results online.

It has been revealed that elk face other health threats too. Earth.com has reported on an emerging hoof disease that may change how elk bodies work.

The areas remain open to park visitors during the program, the Park Service says, and visitors are “strongly encouraged to wear bright colors.”.

Park Service and Wyoming Game and Fish staff patrol the area to check that hunters follow the rules and to share information about bear safety.

Recent findings suggest that hunters are not the only pressure on elk in the region. In nearby Yellowstone, research suggests cougars pose an even bigger threat to elk than wolves.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service news release 2026 Elk Reduction Program begins November 14 in Grand Teton National Park (November 6, 2026) and Grand Teton National Park’s Elk Reduction Area 75 page.

In 1958, the Hope Diamond went to the Smithsonian by mail for $2.44 in postage, and the museum claims a jeweler likely embellished its curse to sell it

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A jeweler's employee paid $145.29 to mail the 45.52-carat blue gem from Newly introduced York, nearly all of it to insure it for $1 million.
  • In a recent development, on November 8, 1958, an employee of Harry Winston’s jewelry store in New York City mailed an ordinary-looking package.
  • According to recent reports, the employee paid $145.29 to send it to the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., according to the Smithsonian’s National Postal Museum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A jeweler's employee paid $145.29 to mail the 45.52-carat blue gem from Newly introduced York, nearly all of it to insure it for $1 million.

In a recent development, on November 8, 1958, an employee of Harry Winston’s jewelry store in New York City mailed an ordinary-looking package. Inside was the Hope Diamond.

According to recent reports, the employee paid $145.29 to send it to the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., according to the Smithsonian’s National Postal Museum. Only $2.44 of that was postage. The rest paid for $1 million in insurance.

The 45.52-carat blue diamond traveled by registered mail in a plain brown wrapper. It is still on display at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History, and the museum has a short answer for anyone who asks whether it carries a curse.

Sources indicate that “Is the Hope Diamond cursed? Of course not!” the museum indicates on its history of the gem.

In Washington, local letter carrier James G. Todd picked up the package at the city post office, a building that now houses the National Postal Museum.

Leonard Carmichael, the Secretary of the Smithsonian, brought Todd into the Gem Hall, where reporters and cameras watched him pull the package from his mail satchel and hand it over, the Postal Museum recounts.

Recent findings suggest that the Natural History Museum dates the arrival to November 10, 1958. Harry Winston’s wife presented the diamond to Carmichael and to George S. Switzer, the museum’s curator of mineralogy. It “almost immediately became its premier attraction,” according to the museum.

It has been revealed that the diamond’s history is far older. The Smithsonian traces it to a blue diamond of about 115 carats known as Tavernier’s Diamond, after the French merchant Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, which King Louis XIV had recut.

It must have come from India, the museum notes, since India was the only commercial source of diamonds in Tavernier’s time.

Sources indicate that the curse is much younger. “The story of a curse is a recent part of the diamond’s history, apparently having its origins in the early 20th century,” the museum says.

One early account ran in the Washington Post in January 1908. According to the Smithsonian, it offered “a selective history” of the gem, listing the bad luck of earlier owners. Later versions of the curse followed the same pattern.

A November 1909 newspaper report that a former owner, the Turkish diamond merchant Selim Habib, had drowned with the gem when a steamer sank at Singapore added to the legend.

The museum calls that report “wildly inaccurate.” Neither Habib nor the diamond was on the ship, and he had already sold the stone in June 1909.

The Smithsonian says some of the people who spread the curse stories may have done so for their own gain.

The French jewelry house Cartier bought the Hope Diamond in 1910, and Pierre Cartier set out to sell it. Intriguing histories helped sell gems in those years.

“Cartier thus began to fabricate a fanciful story around the Hope Diamond that included a curse, which he would pitch to potential buyers,” the museum writes.

According to recent reports, he pitched it to Ned and Evalyn Walsh McLean, and the sale took two years. In the Smithsonian’s words, Cartier “likely embellished the stories as a sales tactic.”.

The tale did not scare Evalyn McLean off. She told Cartier she believed objects that brought bad luck to others would bring good luck to her.

After he had the stone reset and left it with the couple for a weekend, she agreed to buy it in 1912 for $180,000 plus the return of a pendant she no longer wanted.

May Yohé, who was once married to Lord Francis Hope, an earlier owner, helped make the curse a popular modern legend.

In a book and a film released in 1921, she blamed the diamond for her failed marriage and the loss of the Hope family fortune, according to the Smithsonian.

Industry observers note that after Evalyn McLean died in 1947, Harry Winston bought her jewelry, including the Hope Diamond, in 1949. He demonstrated it across the United States in a traveling exhibition called the Court of Jewels before giving it to the Smithsonian.

At the donation ceremony, Winston’s wife scoffed at the idea of a curse and noted that her family had held the gem without any ill effects.

Todd, the letter carrier, had a harder time. Within a year of the delivery, he was hurt in two separate car accidents, his wife died of a heart attack, his dog strangled on its leash and his home in Seat Pleasant, Maryland, was partly destroyed by fire, according to the Postal Museum.

In a recent development, he still did not blame the diamond. “I don’t believe any of that stuff,” he told a reporter.

“If the hex is supposed to affect the owners, then the public should be having the bad luck,” he added.

The diamond stayed at the Natural History Museum, and the brown paper wrapper it came in is now part of the National Postal Museum’s collection.

The Hope’s deep blue color has its own science story. Earth.com has reported that some blue diamonds formed hundreds of miles below Earth’s surface.

The Smithsonian has hidden history of its own, including a secret chamber from 1847 found beneath the Smithsonian Castle.

The information was obtained from the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History’s History of the Hope Diamond and the National Postal Museum’s Delivering the Hope Diamond.
