The 9 Best Binoculars, According to Our Tests and Research

📅 18 Oct 2019 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4288 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • It has been revealed that despite ubiquitous satellite imagery, incredible smartphone cameras, and a video doorbell on almost every house, there’s still incredible power in witnessing something with your own eyes.
  • Hunters use binoculars to spot and pick out details on their quarry thousands of yards away, birders confirm species they’re identifying, and stargazers zoom in on constellations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that despite ubiquitous satellite imagery, incredible smartphone cameras, and a video doorbell on almost every house, there’s still incredible power in witnessing something with your own eyes. Unfortunately, despite eyesight being our dominant sense, our optics have some real limitations. Binoculars are considered relatively old technology, but they’re still recognized as the best tool to reach for when identifying a far-off animal or examining details on a backyard bird.

Hunters use binoculars to spot and pick out details on their quarry thousands of yards away, birders confirm species they’re identifying, and stargazers zoom in on constellations. They’re also just handy to keep in your house or even your vehicle for those moments when you just want to “see for yourself.”.

Sources indicate that you can extend your vision with telescopes, spotting scopes, and even zoom camera lenses, but the comfort and ease of use are why binoculars have such enduring appeal. Monocular devices—spotting scopes, for instance—can put strain on your eyes after only a few minutes, while binoculars offer a much more natural extension of normal vision, making them more comfortable for long sessions and easier for beginners to use. Binoculars are also lighter than those similar devices, which makes them packable and portable for trips into nature where they offer a more intimate look at shy creatures.

The challenge in shopping for a pair of binoculars is the sheer number and diversity of options from major, high-powered zooms that require a tripod to pocket-sized budget versions and everything in between. To help you narrow your search, we dive into how to select a pair that fits within your price range and how you intend to use them. We also share our favorites from years of testing in the field.

Industry observers note that I’m a lifelong hunter and wildlife enthusiast who uses binoculars year-round for hunting as well as volunteer wildlife surveys for bighorn sheep and goats. Long hours behind glass, as well as more than a decade of testing dozens of pairs of binoculars in the field for editorial reviews, have informed my picks, along with conversations with brand representatives and optics dealers. For this enhancement of my long-running guide, I tested six newly introduced pairs of binoculars that are new releases from established optics brands. Not all of them made the cut here, but several did, including the Nikon Trailblazer II 10x25, the first time I enjoyed a microcompact binocular enough to include it.

Industry observers note that the new Leupold BX-3 Alpine HD binoculars deliver premium-enough outdoor optics while maintaining a price point almost everyone can stomach. The BX-2 Alpine HD, which occupied that exact niche for years, did it well enough that it became my favorite binocular in the midrange category and my everyday hunting optic.

This is a compact, lightweight binocular with good clarity and low-light performance, which makes it a solid choice for basically everyone from birders to stargazers, even though Leupold tends to market mostly to hunters and target shooters. While not the cheapest bino on the market, it’s worth the upgrade over the lowest-tier optics and, like any Leupold optic, comes with a lifetime warranty, meaning it could conceivably be the last pair you’ll ever buy.

The BX-3 doesn’t reinvent anything, but Leupold subtly refined the binos, updating coatings, tweaking ergonomics, and adding a few quality-of-life improvements while keeping the same general form factor, magnification options, and modest price point that made the BX-2 so successful in the first place.

The price jumped up slightly with the release of the BX-3, so while I’d buy the BX-3 for the improvements if you’re paying full price, retailers appear to be deeply discounting the existing stock of BX-2s, so it’s worth considering the older model if there’s a great price on it, at least until retailers run out of the now-discontinued model.

Read the Full Review of the Leupold BX-3 Here.

It has been revealed that zeiss is synonymous with good glass in consumer camera lenses and sport optics, so the mid-tier-priced Terra ED 10x42 binoculars are somewhat of a surprise in the manufacturer’s lineup. I’ve tested several higher-end Zeiss binoculars, which were unsurprisingly great given their price tags, but finding nearly as good clarity and color in this $500 pair was unexpected.

While $500 isn’t cheap for most casual binocular buyers, I’d argue getting Zeiss quality at this price presents a serious value if you’re looking for good glass but aren’t ready to put down a mortgage payment to get it.

The 10x42 Terra ED uses ED glass and Zeiss's hydrophobic multicoating to produce a bright, high-contrast image that will feel like a serious upgrade to budget options. It's not going to match the edge-to-edge perfection or low-light performance of Zeiss's flagship binoculars, but it delivers enough optical quality to be an obvious jump in clarity for the investment.

The 10x42 configuration is a versatile middle ground for hunting, hiking, birding, and general wildlife observation. The Terra ED has a 330-foot field of view at 1,000 yards and a 5.3-foot close focus, so it is adequate for birding, casual stargazing, and wildlife watching. At 25.6 ounces, it's also light enough to carry comfortably in a chest harness (not included) for long stretches without pulling on your neck.

The fiberglass-reinforced housing is waterproof and nitrogen-filled to minimize fog and condensation outdoors. The hydrophobic coating helps keep moisture from becoming a major distraction when you're using the binoculars in wet weather or going between temperature extremes. The large focus wheel is also easy to find and operate rapidly.

The Terra ED isn't the cheapest 10x42 on the market, but that's not really the point. It's a relatively affordable way into a serious optics brand, and the difference is visible when you use them side by side with cheaper binos.

Most hunters don't need the biggest or most expensive binoculars they can buy, but many with the budget and obsession with the sport will spend thousands hoping expensive optics can buy success. While $3,000 binoculars are overkill for most, hunters do ask a lot of their optics. Early morning and late evening light and long distances expose the weaknesses of lower-quality glass, so many hunters get the advice to buy the best glass they can afford.

According to recent reports, while the top-tier binoculars are undoubtedly better, there’s a mid-tier sweet spot that gives you most of the performance of those four-figure binos at a fraction of the price. The Vortex Viper HD 10x42 binoculars are squarely there. Vortex’s Triumph binoculars are our Best Budget pick above for the value they provide at $100, but dedicated hunters who get up early and stay out late will eventually want to upgrade.

The Viper HD 10x42s have a list price around $729, but can be found at most retailers for closer to $500, a good value for the upgrade. Still, that’s $400 more than the Triumph, so you’ll want to be sure you value the improvements. The benefits over cheaper options are better light transmission and reduced distortions such as chromatic aberrations. If you’ve used cheaper binos, you’ve seen off colors such as purple fringes on trees. In broad daylight, this isn’t a problem you can’t adjust your eyes to, but in low light and longer distances it can result in straining and struggling to tell a stump from a bear or deer.

A relatively low 24.9-ounce weight and compact form factor enabled by the roof prism design make these comfortable to carry in a chest harness over long days in the field or a tree stand. The rubber housing offers satisfactory grip and I notably appreciated the underside thumb grooves, though they don’t look as high-end as magnesium housings. The included chest harness is capable enough, but will be a throwaway for hunters who already own a specialized hunting chest rig.

Turned off by cheap compact binoculars in the past? These are worth it. They offer quality optics with powerful-enough magnification for bird-watching, hunting, and a range of everyday uses. In addition, they’re sealed, so they're waterproof and fogproof, and there is a lifetime warranty on the optical parts so you won’t need to replace them if you drop these binos even once.

Nikon’s Trailblazer II 10x25 compact binoculars make some compromises on field of view and low-light performance, but on the plus side, they’re small enough to fit in your pocket. These are binoculars you can toss in a daypack for when you want them, rather than committing to positioning them on you, front and center, and dealing with the weight.

Industry observers note that the trade-off, however, is the 25mm objective lens. There's simply less glass available to gather light than you'll get with a 42mm binocular, and the field of view isn’t bad but feels cramped if you’re used to bigger binos. The 10mm eye relief also isn't particularly generous for eyeglass wearers. But for quick looks during daylight, the compact size makes these much easier to have on you when you need them.

Industry observers note that bigger is typically better when it comes to optical performance in binoculars, but there is always a give-and-take. With standard 10x42 or larger binoculars, you get better performance, but usually at least a pound of weight and a bulky item. Bird-watchers and hunters use chest harnesses to distribute the weight and keep them accessible, but that’s a commitment you don’t always want for a casual hike.

The Trailblazer II has a more palatable price at $130 than you’ll find with larger binos with similar optical quality, making these a no-brainer if you’re shopping for casual use.

Recent findings suggest that like Leupold, Vortex has a great reputation, in large part due to its accommodating lifetime warranty program—a comfort to those of us who are hard on our gear. One challenge with Vortex is the sheer number of lines and models, but the newer Triumph line is easy to understand: it’s the brand’s cheapest pair of binoculars in the 10x42 build and arguably its best value at $100. While the optical clarity and quality aren’t on par with that of the more expensive lines, the Triumph does surprisingly well, especially in daylight.

Like most cheaper binos, the clarity falls off the closer you get to the edges of the field of view, but is sharp and color-true in the center. Yes, you can spend less, but I wouldn’t recommend it, having tried a lot of $25 to $50 binoculars over the years. Despite the attractive price, the Triumph ships with a case, harness, and neck strap as well.

Full Vortex Triumph 10x42 Binoculars Review.

Nikon is best known for its cameras and lenses, but this Japanese optics brand makes a wide range of excellent binoculars as well. I’ve tested several models over the years, but the Monarch M7 stands out for the optical clarity it delivers at a mid-tier price point.

Recent findings suggest that nearly any pair of binoculars will work for birding, but for most species, you’ll be in trees and fairly close quarters where higher magnifications can make it harder to spot and track birds with the more zoomed-in view. Even when you spot a bird, even the slightly tighter 10x magnification can make it harder to follow flight.

In a recent development, the 8x42 version of the Monarch M7 binos gives you enough magnification to confirm details without spooking wildlife, but the wide field makes it easier to track them. The M5 series is also good and about $200 cheaper, but it has a narrow field of view even in the 8x42 configuration.

Industry observers note that like most binoculars, they’re nitrogen-purged and O-ring sealed, which just means they’re waterproof and fogproof. (Note: Fogproof only means there won’t be interior fog. You can still steam up the glass if, for example, your face is warm and the air or binos are cold.).

According to recent reports, more money can, of course, get you even better glass from Nikon and other companies, but this is one of the best mid-tier options that delivers a clear and comfortable birding experience. Less money will downgrade your clarity, but cheaper and smaller options that weigh and cost much less abound if those are your priorities. (The entry-level Nocs Provisions Standard Problem 8x25 binos, for example, weigh about half as much.).

Recent findings suggest that there are times when 10x binoculars simply aren't enough—and that’s especially true in Western hunting country where the animal you're looking for might be thousands of yards across a canyon. A 15x binocular like Maven's C.4 gives you considerably more reach while retaining the depth perception and comfort of looking through both eyes.

In a recent development, extra reach is the reason to buy these. At 15x, details that can be frustratingly ambiguous through a conventional 10x42 become much easier to pick apart. I've found high-power binoculars particularly useful for searching large expanses of terrain where the ability to use both eyes makes extended glassing considerably more comfortable than squinting through a spotting scope. At distances of a mile or more, you’ll still want a spotter that’s 20x and up, but the 15x is a meaningful middle ground that’s wide enough to use in a forest, but reaches far enough for substantial mountain hunting.

The C.4 combines 15x magnification with large 56mm objective lenses, giving it a 215-foot field of view at 1,000 yards. This is noticeably tighter than, for example, the 342-foot field of view of the Leupold BX-3 10x42s, but that’s by design and the trade-off for 50 percent more zoom.

Industry observers note that the other significant trade-off is the weight and size. At 45 ounces, they’re still lighter than a spotting scope, but you’ll likely also be carrying a tripod, which adds several pounds to your pack. Compare this to 10x42s, which are usually 1 to 2 pounds total, and it’s a big difference. Still, if you’re using binoculars to cover big mountain distances and need the clarity and zoom to identify animals precisely, it’s likely a weight penalty you’ll be willing to pay.

Sources indicate that the ED glass and phase-corrected, dielectric-coated prisms produce a surprisingly sharp image, and the 92 percent light transmission is key around dawn and dusk—impressive for the price. Most high-quality, high-power binoculars are at least four figures, but Maven delivers the C.4 for $550. Unlike the rest of its line that uses Japanese and Chinese components that are assembled in Wyoming, the C.4 is produced entirely in China. Despite this difference, I didn’t notice a sharp drop-off in build or optical quality from other Maven binos I’ve tested.

In a recent development, there's a catch: These aren't really handheld binoculars. At 45.1 ounces, the C.4 is almost twice the weight of many conventional 10x42s, and 15x magnification makes even small hand movements obvious. I used the C.4 handheld fine for short periods, but the size and weight wear on your stability much faster than lightweight hunting binos. Once mounted, however, the extra weight only affects your pack and the C.4 becomes a remarkably capable long-distance optic.

According to recent reports, any decent pair of binoculars can enhance casual stargazing, but if you’re closer to “astrophile” than “occasional noticer of the night sky,” you’ll want a somewhat specialized pair and the best low-light performance you can afford. As binoculars go up in price, into the thousands, the returns are diminishing, giving you small increments of improved clarity and edge-case benefits, but they are better.

Recent findings suggest that celestron is a budget binocular brand, but its SkyMaster series is astro-focused and worth a look if you’re focused on stars. The massive objective lenses, high magnification, and Porro prism combine for a heavy build, but one that’s designed for night use at the distance of light-years.

The 25x magnification won’t be much good for backyard bird-watching or any handheld use, but they’re designed for tripod mounting, and for use as a stationary sky-watching setup that’s more comfortable for longer sessions than telescopes.

Going with binoculars for sky watching, especially ones as zoomed-in as these, adds a layer of dimensionality that’s lost looking with the naked eye (or with one eye as with telescopes). Unlike cheap Amazon optics brands, Celestron has friendly price points but still gives you a lifetime warranty. If your stargazing habit sticks, you may eventually want to upgrade to a higher-end model, but this pair will show you what you’ve been missing for a few hundred bucks.

It has been revealed that yes, this is an article about binoculars, but I humbly present the little-known monocular as a better tool for certain jobs. Like spotting scopes, monoculars aren’t as natural to use since you have to close one eye and miss out on the depth of a stereo picture. However, there are times when the weight and bulk of binos mean you leave them at home even though you might want them in the field.

I personally carry this Nocs Field Tube monocular every time I go backcountry skiing and find it quite literally worth its weight for scouting potential approach and descent lines, using it to pick out details about snow quality, avalanches, and terrain that my naked eye regularly misses. It’s also easy to throw in a pack or pocket for casual hikes or pre-hunting season scouting walks where I never know when I might want a closer look at something but am not motivated enough to harness up with my binoculars.

There aren’t a lot of companies making monoculars, but Nocs has several options. I love the 8x32 size of the Field Tube, but you can get a 10x32 version that offers a bit more zoom but a slightly narrower field of view in the same size package. There’s also the newer 8x32 Zoom Tube that’s significantly cheaper and slightly lighter and smaller but isn’t fully waterproof.

In a recent development, not everything we test or like ends up in our buying guide, but some are products that still warrant a mention. Here are a few.

Sources indicate that vortex Crossfire HD 10x42: These budget binos fall between the Triumph and Viper models we recommend above. They’re solid optics for the cost, but in a no-man’s-land for the price. If you’re on a tight budget, the Triumph 10x42s are less than half the price and nearly as good. And if you’re looking to upgrade to the mid-tier, it’s worth saving up for the Vipers or the Zeiss Terra ED 10x42s for a more noticeable jump in quality in a compact all-arounder.Nocs Field Glitch 10x42: Give us some fun colors and a grippy, overmolded texture like on these 10x42s. But similar to the Vortex Crossfire, they’re not enough of an improvement on our best budget pick to justify double the cost. If you like the design that stands out from a crowd of bland black options, you won’t be disappointed, but we prefer to pay for performance.Zeiss SFL 12x50: These are awesome high-end binoculars that pack a little extra zoom as well as a large, 50mm objective lens that pulls in extra light for early and late. They also are incredibly compact and light despite their specs. The problem is the $2,000 price tag that puts them out of reach of most casual users. They’re really good, just not 10 times as good as a solid $200 pair from our list above.

In a recent development, the magnifications of most consumer binoculars are fixed (i.e., not zoomable), making it one of the most crucial decisions for buyers. More isn't always better and can feel claustrophobic in tight quarters such as trying to track a small bird in dense forest, while wider-angle, lower-power lenses can feel underpowered if you're trying to see across longer distances.

Most binos range between 7x and 18x. Much less than 7x isn’t enough of an effect to bother with for most applications, while 15x and up becomes difficult to use without a tripod. In general, lower-power binoculars are a better fit if you’re mostly glassing shorter distances, such as in forests, and don’t need precise detail. Higher-power binoculars make sense if you’re looking to avoid also carrying a spotting scope and glassing longer distances up to a mile or need precise detail for identifying wildlife.

Objective lens diameter is the size of the lens farthest from your eyes and impacts the field of vision you get, as well as how bright the image is since, generally, bigger lenses capture more light. Jeremy Bentham, senior manager of SRO Sales & Operations for Nikon, explains the trade-offs associated with objective lens size.

Recent findings suggest that “One of the key things that needs to be decided is brightness versus weight,” he says. “Larger objective lenses allow more light into the optic but are also heavier to pack and carry with you.”.

Objective lens sizes in binoculars range anywhere from 20 mm to 100 mm, but the common sizes are mostly in the 30 mm to 60 mm range. I find ultracompact binoculars of less than about 30 mm annoying to use for more than a quick look at something nearby since the field of view is small and it can be harder to keep in position on your eyes. On the other end of the spectrum, most binoculars larger than about 55 mm become heavy and unwieldy if used without a tripod.

Sources indicate that binoculars are listed by size spec, where the first number is magnification and the second is objective lens diameter. Probably the most common size is 10x42, which permits a significant enough field of view and magnification for viewing things as near as 15 feet but still allows you to spot larger objects such as wildlife as far as a mile away.

For backcountry hunters and hikers, weight is one of the most vital considerations in a binocular. You need to balance the desire for a larger, brighter optic with your ability and interest to carry it around your neck over long distances. For me, anything heavier than about 35 ounces is too much to carry in a chest harness when actively hunting and covering several miles a day. If you’re a hunter or hiker who doesn’t need ready access to your binoculars and can keep them in a pack until you need them at specific spots, you may be able to tolerate heavier options.

It has been revealed that even folks who mostly use binoculars at home or from a vehicle need to consider weight. Heavier binoculars are harder to use for longer periods of time since your arms and shoulders do eventually fatigue and become shaky. If you’re mostly using binoculars on a tripod (a must for higher-magnification binos), you may want to prize optical quality over weight savings.

In a recent development, aside from range-finding binoculars, most have surprisingly little tech as we usually think of it in terms of electronics and connectivity. What makes great binoculars hasn’t changed much over the years and still boils down to quality glass and craftsmanship.

Industry observers note that where tech does show up is in the glass quality and the coatings used. High-tech coatings are used to make colors true, enhance brightness, and protect your expensive lenses. Coatings and glass often use nonstandardized terms such as ED, HD, and UHD glass, or proprietary branding such as LotuTec or Swarobright, making it hard to compare apples to apples when talking about something as subjective as optical quality. What you can look for is whether lenses are “fully multi-coated,” meaning that all glass surfaces have multiple coatings for durability and performance, whatever the branding.

Standard fertility tests may be missing an important clue about sperm health

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Retained mitochondrial DNA in mature sperm has been linked to longer times to pregnancy, even among men with normal semen test results.
  • Recent findings suggest that men in couples who struggle to conceive are usually sent for a semen analysis.
  • According to recent reports, A study of 327 men with normal semen results has now pointed to one extra factor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Retained mitochondrial DNA in mature sperm has been linked to longer times to pregnancy, even among men with normal semen test results.

Recent findings suggest that men in couples who struggle to conceive are usually sent for a semen analysis. The test measures sperm count, concentration, shape and movement. Normal results do not guarantee a quick pregnancy.

According to recent reports, A study of 327 men with normal semen results has now pointed to one extra factor. Some of their mature sperm still carried mitochondrial DNA.

This DNA belongs to the mitochondria, the parts of a cell that make energy. Couples needed more time to conceive when the man’s sperm held more of it.

Recent findings suggest that the study was carried out at the Wayne State University School of Medicine in Detroit. It was observational, so a link was found but a cause was not established.

In a recent development, the senior author was J. Richard Pilsner, a professor at Wayne State’s C.S. Mott Center for Human Growth and Development.

“These findings provide an notable latest window into the male contribution to reproductive success,” Pilsner mentioned.

Almost every cell in the body contains mitochondria. Energy for the cell is generated within these small compartments.

Sources indicate that mitochondria contain their own circular DNA, which carries 37 genes. In humans, it is passed on through the mother.

R. E. Giles and colleagues reported this maternal pattern in PNAS in 1980. Defects in these genes underlie several inherited diseases, and mitochondrial donation has been used to prevent their transmission.

Mitochondria are retained by the egg. According to a separate study, women’s egg cells keep this DNA largely free of age-related damage.

In sperm, a different process is assumed. Most paternal mitochondrial DNA is thought to be eliminated during sperm production.

Recent findings suggest that that assumption sat awkwardly beside earlier data. Higher sperm mitochondrial DNA had been associated with lower semen quality and with longer times to pregnancy.

Two sources were proposed for the excess DNA. Ordinary body cells may have contaminated the samples, or immature sperm cells may have been present.

Purified, frozen sperm from the LIFE Study were analyzed by the Wayne State team. Couples in that cohort had been enrolled before conception and followed while they attempted pregnancy.

Recent findings suggest that female partners kept daily journals. Time to pregnancy was then calculated in menstrual cycles.

Inclusion was restricted to men who met the 2010 WHO criteria for sperm count, concentration and shape. Of these, 327 were analyzed.

Mitochondrial DNA was quantified by digital PCR, a method that detects and counts individual copies of a target sequence.

Values ranged from 0.5 copies at the lower end to 49.0 copies at the upper end.

Bulk measurements cannot indicate which cells contain the DNA. Imaging of individual sperm was therefore required.

Samples from 18 men were selected at random, six from each of the low, moderate and high groups. Fluorescence in situ hybridization, which labels a chosen DNA sequence with a glowing tag, was adapted for sperm.

Industry observers note that image scoring was performed blind to group. A total of 50 sperm per participant were assessed.

Signal was located in the midpiece, a segment between the head and the tail. Mitochondria are arranged in a sheath around this segment.

Distinct spots were resolved around the midpiece in three-dimensional microscope images. Signal was not localized to the head or tail.

Jeffrey Mann, the study’s first author, is a postdoctoral fellow at Wayne State. He described the meaning of the images.

“Directly visualizing mitochondrial DNA within the sperm midpiece provides compelling evidence that the mitochondrial DNA detected by polymerase chain reaction reflects DNA retained within mature sperm,” Mann stated.

Men with higher DNA levels had a larger share of glowing sperm. The correlation between the two measures was 0.87, where 1 would be a perfect match.

In men with moderate or high mitochondrial DNA levels, the glowing signals covered a larger area of the sperm midpiece than in men with low levels.

Recent findings suggest that sperm within a single sample differed from one another. In high-group samples, glowing sperm were found beside sperm with no signal.

A high reading appears to reflect a mixed population. Some sperm kept their mitochondrial DNA, while others removed it as expected.

DNA levels were then compared with the time each couple took to conceive. Higher levels were linked to a lower chance of pregnancy per menstrual cycle.

In a recent development, the team reported a fecundability odds ratio of 0.79. Values below 1 indicate lower odds of pregnancy per cycle as levels rise.

In a recent development, differences between the low, moderate and high groups were unlikely to be due to chance. The link remained after adjustment for both partners’ age, body mass index and smoking.

Pilsner linked the imaging and pregnancy results.

“For the first time, we directly visualized mitochondrial DNA retained within mature sperm and demonstrated that this feature is associated with lower likelihood of achieving pregnancy, even among men with normal semen parameters,” Pilsner said.

The team views the measure as a possible addition to routine semen analysis. A separate study found that body fat can lower sperm counts in men of normal weight.

“These findings suggest that conventional semen analysis may miss molecular signatures within sperm that provide key information about couples’ ability to conceive,” Pilsner stated.

Recent findings suggest that the study did not prove that retained DNA slows pregnancy. Only an association was shown.

Industry observers note that men with abnormal semen results were excluded. This limited the influence of other sperm problems on the findings.

The results cannot yet be extended to men with abnormal semen or diagnosed infertility.

Industry observers note that some factors were not measured. These included how often couples had sex, which also affects time to pregnancy.

The probe detects specific DNA sequences. Whether each spot represents a complete mitochondrial genome or a fragment is still unknown.

Industry observers note that imaging was performed on only 18 men. The microscope images have been posted online for other researchers.

It has been revealed that future studies could test a link with TFAM, a protein that packages mitochondrial DNA. Retention in men with abnormal semen results could also be examined.

“This finding opens newly introduced questions about the molecular mechanisms that allow some sperm to retain mitochondrial DNA,” Mann said.

According to recent reports, normal semen results may not give a complete picture of male fertility. Leftover mitochondrial DNA in sperm could be worth measuring alongside the standard tests.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

The 8 Best Electric Scooters Built for the Daily Commute—And Beyond

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Industry observers note that instead of driving for every short trip to the store or commute to work, hop on an electric scooter and zoom through your neighborhood.
  • Sources indicate that these days, there are plenty of affordable and durable electric scooters available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that instead of driving for every short trip to the store or commute to work, hop on an electric scooter and zoom through your neighborhood. Electric scooters are easier to ride than electric skateboards and more portable than electric bikes, so they’re a great alternative for city-dwellers who don’t have the space for a car or would prefer a smaller mode of transportation for short distances.

Sources indicate that these days, there are plenty of affordable and durable electric scooters available. Options range from electric scooters built for just a few miles of daily commuting to ones designed to handle uneven trails, high speeds, and long distances. We tried out electric scooters on our own commutes to find the best.

In a recent development, what Are the Laws for Riding E-Scooters?In many areas, electric scooters aren’t allowed on sidewalks, so check whether you need to ride in bike lanes before you jet around. Some areas have speed limits on small electric vehicles like scooters and e-bikes. For instance, in Florida, e-scooters with seats must be registered and have a title and license plate, so check your local laws before you opt for one of our seated options. Similarly, there are some restrictions based on battery size and type.

If you’re looking for a scooter that can do just about everything well—with a long range to boot—check out the Segway Ninebot Kickscooter Max. It can go up to 40 miles on a single charge, handle slopes up to 22 degrees, and carry riders up to 265 pounds.

It has been revealed that its 10-inch pneumatic tires are great at absorbing bumps in the road, and it folds easily for storage. The tires are “self-sealing,” meaning an interior liner will automatically fill in punctures for a short-term patch. It’s not a permanent solution, but even if you roll over a nail or sharp rock, you’ll be able to continue driving without stopping for an immediate replacement. At just over 40 pounds, this Ninebot is heavier than some commuter scooters. But some of that comes from the bigger battery for extended range.

Industry observers note that while 40 miles won’t take you on long-range adventures, it should last for multiple weeks of scootering around town. The Ninebot is the second most expensive of the scooters we recommend. But considering how well-rounded this e-scooter is, it’s the best for most people.

In a recent development, the GoTrax XR Elite needs to be on your radar if you’re looking for an electric scooter that doesn’t take a bite out of your wallet. At just 32 pounds, it’s one of the lightest and easiest to carry among the scooters here. This is further amplified by the foldable design and slender frame.

It has been revealed that this scooter has an estimated range of 16 miles, a top speed of about 15 miles per hour, and a max incline of 15 degrees. What really sets it apart from the others is the affordable price given the quality performance. This costs about $400 less than the Segway Ninebot Kickscooter Max.

According to recent reports, while the XR Elite isn’t built for long distances or top speeds, it’s a perfect choice for puttering around town. Moreover, its battery charges in just four hours, allowing you to get around sooner if need be.

In a recent development, very few electric scooters offer the balance of affordability and performance that the Gotrax G3 Max does. With a maximum range of 37 miles, the scooter is ideal for daily commuting back and forth to work without the constant need to recharge.

Beyond this, the scooter is equipped with a number of features that caught our eye, including the integrated number lock on the body that dissuades thieves by preventing them from actually being able to unfold and ride the scooter without the right code.

According to recent reports, the G3 Max also comes with an LED display showing your speed, speed modes, mileage, and battery life. There’s an LED headlight for riding at night too.

Full Gotrax G3 Max Electric Scooter Review.

According to recent reports, don’t confuse this electric scooter with a bike or moped. Built with a seat and basket, the Flex Ultra from Gotrax is more than just a quick commuter.

Sources indicate that when testing this scooter, I took it from Central Park all the way back to my apartment in Brooklyn. I had my backpack, which weighed over 20 pounds, in the basket, and I sat on the seat for the majority of the trip.

What I noticed immediately was the zip of the motor as I got close to 20 miles per hour on straightaways and churned up the incline of the Queensboro Bridge without losing momentum. I also have to admit that I loved the seat. Instead of standing for over 30 minutes on the ride back, I could rest a bit more while still making better time than I would on the subway.

The throttle is responsive, and the larger 14-inch wheels stood up well to the potholes on the streets and cracks on the pavement. While its size prevents it from being an easy storage item in a closet—even though it folds—this electric scooter comes with the power, comfort, and convenience for quick grocery trips and long city commutes alike.

With a 34-mile range and a top speed of 20 miles per hour, the Ninebot E3 Pro is an ideal commuter scooter balancing speed and range. It’s also quite durable, with an alloy frame boasting an IPX5 water resistance for riding through puddles, rain, and even mud.

Furthermore, the electric scooter is a relatively quick charge, going from zero to fully charged in 7 hours. This means you can plug it in overnight and ride out in the morning on a full charge with no worry. Alongside an LED headlight, the scooter comes with lighting underneath the board so you’ll have full visibility at night.

The headlight and under-board lighting are paired with real turn signals as well, so you don’t have to take your hands of the handles to let drivers around you know which direction you’re headed.

Full Segway E3 Pro Electric Scooter Review.

This lightweight and affordable scooter won’t take you everywhere with just a 16 mile range, but you can take it anywhere you please. The scooter is small enough to fold up and carry without feeling like it’s dragging on your arm after a few minutes.

While it won’t exactly disappear under a desk, it’s probably one of the few that will fit with ease in a storage closet or under the bed at home. At the same time, you can toss it in the back of your trunk and take it out whenever you go to the park.

The hollow tires also mean you’ll never run flat and don’t need to worry about inflating them after a few winter months out of use.

According to recent reports, have you ever wanted to take a load off while riding but don’t want a permanent seat? The Gotrax Eclipse offers the best of both worlds. The electric scooter comes with a detachable seat so you can plop down if you know you have a long ride ahead, but can take it off and leave it at home when portability and foldability take priority.

According to recent reports, the scooter is more than just the seat as well. With a top speed of 25 miles per hour and a max range of 38 miles, this is a performance-focused option that is great for longer commutes and open streets.

At the same time, the electric scooter has a small rear shelf that can be used to securely tie down small packages and backpacks so you can actually use it for carrying more than just yourself.

Reaching speeds of over 30 miles per hour and boasting a range of 45, this electric scooter from Segway is aptly named the SuperScooter GT3. This heavy-duty option is designed with performance as the end all, be all priority. In fact, in combination with its 11-inch self-sealing tires, the SuperScooter GT3 is one of the few electric scooters that is legitimately well-equipped to handle gravel, dirt, and general off-road adventures.

Beyond pure power and battery, the electric scooter comes with one of the most useful displays that we’ve found. The full color screen comes with smart technology that connects to your phone so you can receive notifications and access navigation routes in real time.

That said, before you click buy, make sure it’s actually legal to ride in your city. Electric scooters of this speed and size are often highly regulated and illegal to ride in densely populated cities across the United States.

According to recent reports, an electric scooter’s range is based on battery and motor size and is impacted by a number of factors, including rider weight, weather conditions, surface type, and incline of the roads you travel on. The ranges we include are based on the manufacturers’ claims, and your real-world use will vary.

Many scooters get up to 10 miles, while some can last for up to 40 miles or more on a single charge. Some have various drive settings that help you get the most juice out of your battery based on the type of ride you’re on. For instance, if you’re trying to conserve power for a longer trip, many options have a low-power or eco mode, which reduces top speed or acceleration for the sake of saving the battery. Furthermore, if you want to extend your scooter range as much as possible, consider routing yourself on smooth flat roads with little incline that don't require lots of stopping and starting.

According to recent reports, most of the e-scooters we recommend top out between 15 and 20 mph. That should be fast enough to zip along city streets and paths without feeling like you’re falling behind.

According to recent reports, the only exception to this speed range is the Navee XT5 electric scooter, which reaches a top speed of 31 mph. However, if you’re seeking a quicker commute or more of a thrill, there are other e-scooters that reach speeds up to 60 mph. We didn’t recommend any of those because many states and cities have banned them or require you to gain an additional license to use them.

Recent findings suggest that electric scooters often have motors with a power rating between 250 and 350 watts. This is enough for most daily city commuting. If you’re a heavier person or expected to ride up steep inclines, you may want to opt for a scooter with a larger, more powerful motor. High wattage motors offer significantly more torque and acceleration but typically come at a premium. Their size also makes them heavier than lower wattage motors, which can make the scooter more cumbersome to carry or transport when not in use.

Recent findings suggest that almost all electric scooters have rubber tires, whether they’re solid, tubeless, or tires with inner tubes. Solid rubber tires are the longest-lasting and are ideal for those making shorter rides on smooth streets, but they also absorb less shock than their tubeless counterparts.

Industry observers note that tires with inner tubes were more common in the past, but we’re starting to see more tubeless and tube-ready tires today. Both tubeless and tube-ready tires can suffer punctures, but offer more cushioning during a ride than solid rubber models.

Sources indicate that if you strategy on riding a scooter in the early morning or night, look for a scooter with good front and rear lights. It’s also a good idea to look for a scooter with a horn or bell to warn bikers, pedestrians, and other scooter riders that you’re approaching. Some high end scooters also come with board lights and turn signals for additional visibility in the dark.

All scooters should have good brakes as well. Some only have them on one wheel, but more powerful scooters that need to decelerate rapidly should have front and back brakes, and possibly a motor brake so you don’t go flying down a hill faster than intended. Motor brakes can also provide some regenerative braking, extending the scooter’s range slightly as you ride.

Recent findings suggest that some other extras to look for on electric scooters are items like seats or baskets. These are great to have if you prefer a seated ride and/or if you blueprint on using the scooter for errands, like grocery shopping.

In selecting these electric scooters, we rode multiple options. We used the scooters in daily work commutes to test their power, speed, range, and comfort over distance. This included trips over long bridges, on steep inclines, and many times, on streets without bike lanes. We also gauged how the acceleration and brakes felt in our hands, and how smooth the scooter stayed when riding over bumps or uneven asphalt.

Industry observers note that for scooters we haven’t tested yet, we based our picks on research, evaluating the opinions and ratings of professional reviewers, as well as checking out customer reviews and rankings, and evaluating each model’s most vital specs like wattage, range, and safety features. We chose reputable brands, selecting electric scooters that are not only the highest-performing models on the market, but also the easiest to find in stock.

#157484. The prickly pear cactus has a surprising trick for surviving in the desert

The prickly pear cactus has a surprising trick for surviving in the desert

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1316 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have discovered that tiny, short-lived leaves help prickly pear cacti capture carbon during the day and accelerate growth.
  • Cacti are usually described as plants that replaced their leaves with spines and thick green stems.
  • When rain finally reaches the desert, though, the prickly pear sprouts small green leaves on each fresh pad.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have discovered that tiny, short-lived leaves help prickly pear cacti capture carbon during the day and accelerate growth.

Cacti are usually described as plants that replaced their leaves with spines and thick green stems.

When rain finally reaches the desert, though, the prickly pear sprouts small green leaves on each fresh pad. Within a few weeks, these are shed again.

A team in Israel found that these leaflets behave like the leaves of a common garden plant. Carbon dioxide is taken in by them during the day.

The researchers estimate that they supply about a fifth of the carbon a young pad needs for growth.

So the cactus has two ways of gathering carbon rather than one. Older pads collect it after sunset, and the leaflets add to the supply once the sun is up.

The research was conducted by scientists at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (BGU) in Israel. They worked with researchers from the Gilat Research Center of the Volcani Institute.

Potted plants of Opuntia ficus-indica were grown for the experiments. This is the prickly pear species that is cultivated on farms.

It has been revealed that the plants were kept in a net house on BGU’s desert campus at Sde Boker. They were watered every day for a year.

Ilya Gelfand is a professor at BGU’s Jacob Blaustein Institutes for Desert Research and a co-author of the study.

Recent findings suggest that “The cactus effectively has two gears,” said Gelfand. “Most of the year it runs in saving mode and breathes at night to hold on to every drop.”.

“When water arrives, it switches on a second, faster gear: temporary leaves that work by day like a regular plant. When the good times end, it simply drops them.”.

In most plants the tiny pores on the leaves are opened during the day.

Industry observers note that carbon dioxide enters through them and is used by the plant to build sugars. Water is lost through the same openings, and that loss becomes costly in hot desert conditions.

In a recent development, cacti, agave and many other succulents get by on less water because their pores open at night instead. The carbon dioxide is stored as an acid until the following morning.

The pores then close, and carbon dioxide released from the stored acid is used to make sugars with the help of sunlight.

This strategy is known as crassulacean acid metabolism or CAM. Mature prickly pear pads rely on it so heavily that scientists classify the species as a full-time CAM plant.

The prickly pear is also an key crop that is grown on about 6.4 million acres (2.6 million hectares) worldwide.

It has been revealed that much of this area lies in drought-prone parts of Africa and South America. In these regions the plant is used for food and livestock feed and for slowing desertification.

Recent findings suggest that until this project, nobody had examined the leaflets as working organs. Each one measures only about 0.4 inch (10 millimeters) in length.

Around 150 of them can be carried by a single latest pad, and they fall off after about six weeks.

In a recent development, the study was led by Patrick Mdemba, who is a doctoral student at BGU. Pores were the first thing he and his colleagues examined.

Clear nail polish was brushed onto pads and leaflets at five different times of the day. After the polish had dried it was peeled away and examined under a microscope. Each thin film preserved an impression of the pore openings.

Recent findings suggest that the older pads opened their pores at night, which was the expected result for a CAM plant. The leaflets demonstrated the opposite pattern. Their pores were opened in the morning and closed after dark, as in a typical leafy plant.

Young pads that were two weeks old did not follow either pattern. Their pores were found to be open at every time the team checked.

It has been revealed that acid build-up between dusk and dawn was then measured in each tissue. A large amount was stored overnight in the older pads.

Industry observers note that the young pads stored more acid as they grew older. In the leaflets no significant difference was seen between the dawn and dusk readings.

Mdemba’s team also looked at the carbon inside the leaflets. Carbon in nature comes in a lighter form and a heavier form. Cactus pads that feed at night build up more of the heavier one.

In week-old leaflets the carbon looked much like the carbon in the pads. The mother pad had probably supplied it. Five weeks later the leaflets held noticeably more of the lighter form that daytime leaves collect.

For a second test the researchers sealed whole plants in a clear box almost 4 feet wide. They filled it with carbon dioxide made from the heavier form. One run lasted from 10 a.m. until noon, after the pads had closed their pores.

The marked carbon was found in the leaflets. The pads on those same plants gained no significant amount.

It has been revealed that next came leaflets with no pad at all. Mdemba cut them from pads less than a week old and kept them in sealed jars on a sugar-free gel.

It has been revealed that in sunlight the carbon dioxide in each jar went down. Under aluminum foil it went back up. The cut leaflets also grew heavier until about day 15.

Mature pads in an earlier study took in carbon dioxide about twice as fast per square inch as the leaflets.

Mature pads in an earlier study took in carbon dioxide about twice as fast per square inch.

The team then worked out a carbon budget. A pad with about 150 leaflets gets roughly 0.12 grams of carbon a day from them. A 1998 study put a growing pad’s daily need near 0.6 grams. So the leaflets supply about 20% of it.

The leaflets covered their own growth first. What was left over went to the young pad.

Industry observers note that mdemba then took the leaflets away. All of them were cut off some young pads. On other pads they were left on but painted with clear nail polish, which sealed their pores.

Sources indicate that pad size was checked every five days. By day 25 both groups were about a third smaller in area than normal pads. Pads with no leaflets also weighed about 38% less at three weeks.

Without working leaflets, then, a fresh pad grew more slowly.

“That lets the cactus grow promptly whenever the desert briefly allows it, without giving up its ability to survive drought,” stated Gelfand.

Desert rain tends to arrive in short bursts. For desert plants the timing of that water can matter a great deal.

Industry observers note that some desert shrubs drop their leaves when life gets hard. The prickly pear makes its leaflets in the wet weeks and drops them within about two months.

Every plant in the study got water daily. That may have made the leaflets look more notable than they would be in a dry field. Well-watered pads may rely less on their night feeding.

The authors listed other limits too. They did not measure the two enzymes that capture carbon in each system. Gas exchange was not followed over a full 24 hours. Their conclusions come from pores, acid and carbon tracers instead.

They recommend measuring those enzymes in leaflets and young pads, along with gas readings around the clock.

Sources indicate that plants under drought stress should be tested as well. That work could show how much the leaflets matter when a wet spell is short.

The full study was published in the Journal of Experimental Botany.

Older adults don’t need to lift heavy weights to build strength

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1198 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Strength training with lighter weights may help older adults build strength and maintain muscle mass without heavy lifting.
  • Strength training is recommended for older adults to help maintain muscle, balance and independence.
  • According to recent reports, earlier research has reported that pain and high physical demands can lead older adults to drop out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Strength training with lighter weights may help older adults build strength and maintain muscle mass without heavy lifting.

Strength training is recommended for older adults to help maintain muscle, balance and independence. Heavy loads are commonly used in these programs.

According to recent reports, earlier research has reported that pain and high physical demands can lead older adults to drop out. The authors note that those who drop out often have traits associated with frailty.

According to recent reports, A pilot trial in Perth, Western Australia, compared heavy training with lighter training in 40 adults over 55. Strength increased in both groups over 12 weeks.

Neither group showed a measurable change in muscle mass.

Sources indicate that the study was led by Brett Buist of the School of Human Sciences at the University of Western Australia. Training intensity was chosen by the participants rather than assigned at random.

“Both high- and lower-intensity resistance exercise appears equally effective at improving muscle strength while maintaining muscle mass and quality of life in older adults,” Buist noted.

Frailty has been linked to falls, hospital admissions, disability and death. Low physical activity and the loss of muscle mass and strength are listed among its common contributors.

The condition is not always permanent. Ohio State University’s guide to frailty states that it can often be slowed or improved with support.

Low strength is reflected in poorer walking and balance. These changes are known to raise the risk of a fall in older adults.

Recent findings suggest that world Health Organization figures cited in the paper put the share of people over 60 at 12% in 2015. That share is projected to reach 22% by 2050.

Lifting weights appears on the National Institute on Aging’s list of strength exercises. The Perth study examined how heavy those weights need to be.

Sources indicate that of the 40 recruits, 33 were women. All participants were living independently in the community.

Sessions were held twice a week at the university under the supervision of exercise physiologists or physiotherapists. Every session included a leg press, a deadlift and a bench press.

According to recent reports, drop jumps from a low box were also performed in each session. The box was about 4 inches (10 centimeters) high, and each landing delivered a firm impact through both feet.

A four-week introductory phase at low-to-moderate intensity was completed by all participants. From week five each person could either move to the heavy program or continue at the lighter level.

In both groups the sets were ended while two to five more repetitions could still have been completed.

The number of sets multiplied by repetitions was matched closely between the two programs. In this way the load on the bar remained the main difference.

To be classified as a heavy lifter, a participant had to leg press more than 80% of their estimated maximum. That level had to be reached in at least three out of every four sessions.

Twelve participants met this standard and 14 trained at the lighter level.

By the end of the trial both groups were able to press more weight with their chests and legs. Strength was assessed using the one-repetition maximum, which is the heaviest weight a person can lift once.

Recent findings suggest that increases in chest press, leg press and leg press relative to body weight were found in each group. Substantial loads were still handled by the lighter group.

In a recent development, leg press loads in that group averaged about 71% of maximum. Deadlift effort was rated at a median of 5 on a 10-point scale.

Earlier reviews of research in older adults have generally favored heavy lifting for building strength. In some of the studies behind them, heavy training was compared with loads as low as 20% of maximum.

According to recent reports, according to Buist’s team, loads that low were probably insufficient to increase strength. Unequal amounts of total work have also complicated earlier comparisons.

Leg press strength relative to body weight was the only outcome that differed significantly between the groups. However, the authors advised caution when interpreting this result.

“Clinicians can target factors that contribute to frailty using resistance exercise with intensity tailored to individual preferences without compromising outcomes,” remarked Buist.

Recent findings suggest that neither group showed a measurable gain in muscle. Lean mass measured by whole-body X-ray scans stayed close to baseline in both programs.

This stability was viewed by the researchers as a useful result because lean mass usually declines with age.

Lean tissue already accounted for about 64% of the volunteers’ body weight at the start. This proportion was higher than in a comparison study cited by the authors.

According to recent reports, no protein supplements were provided during the trial. The training volume was modest as well, with 12 working sets in each session. Some studies that did produce muscle growth used as many as 39 sets.

Sources indicate that A small reduction in body fat as a share of total weight was observed in the lighter group. Higher general health scores on the SF-36 survey were reported by the heavy group.

Recent findings suggest that other scores on the questionnaire changed very little in either group. Most volunteers began between the 50th and 75th percentiles for Australians of their age and sex.

Recent findings suggest that postural sway was measured on a force plate during standing trials of 30 seconds each. After training the recorded sway path was longer under some of the test conditions.

In a recent development, A longer sway path is normally taken as a sign of poorer balance. However, scores on the 14-item Berg Balance Scale did not decline and balance confidence was maintained.

Industry observers note that the authors suggest that participants may have been exploring their limits of stability. Resistance training is known to extend those limits.

The participants who completed the trial were not the group of greatest concern. Of the 39 people tested at baseline, 12 withdrew for reasons including joint pain and holidays.

Sources indicate that an average baseline weight of about 162 pounds (73.7 kilograms) was recorded for those who withdrew. Participants who stayed averaged 133 pounds (60.4 kilograms) and had greater leg strength relative to body weight.

Heavier and weaker adults are of particular concern in frailty research, and they were overrepresented among the dropouts.

The final analysis included only 26 people, so small differences between the groups may have been missed. Physical activity outside the supervised sessions was not recorded.

Bonnie Furzer, a co-author from the University of Western Australia, presented the findings as guidance for those who prescribe exercise.

“For older adults who are not tolerating high-intensity resistance and impact training, lowering exercise intensity should be considered to assist adherence whilst maintaining benefits,” said Furzer.

Longer trials and studies in frail adults have been recommended by the authors.

Until that evidence is available, a weight that people continue to lift may matter more than the heaviest one possible.

The full study was published in the journal Translational Exercise Biomedicine.

Sebnem Ece Eksi did a double take. Proteins typically studied in the brain were turning up in prostate cancer cells from high-risk patients. These proteins, called neuronal adhesion molecules, play a key role in the circuitry associated with memory.

The finding, made during her Ph.D. days at the University of Illinois Chicago, raised so many questions to which Eksi is still seeking answers. Now at the Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, Eksi has made it her lab’s goal to find out how nervous systems communicate with cancer. What were once two separate fields might be connected more closely than previously thought.

Recent findings suggest that “What we’re learning is that tumors are actively communicating with the nervous system,” Eksi says. “In a way, it makes sense to me that a growing tumor in our bodies, in an organ, would be immediately sensed and detected by the nervous system.”.

Eksi now intends to test an AI image-based recognition algorithm to identify nerve fibers in human patients. This is exciting, she says, because these nerves aren’t normally visible in patient tumors. But through biopsies, she hopes to map out and observe how the nervous system — which impacts sleep, cognition and pain — changes as cancer progresses. The implications are significant, she says. Could experts use the nervous system to detect cancer early? Can they improve patients’ quality of life?

It has been revealed that “This field of cancer neuroscience can change all different stages of cancer diagnosis and treatments,” Eksi claims. “It’s growing so quickly, the field itself.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family confirmed.
  • In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call).

Sources indicate that former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family confirmed.

In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

According to recent reports, “Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”.

When McDermott confirmed his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”.

Born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

Industry observers note that he attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

He continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against new sanctions on Iran.

Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a fresh life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

“I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”.

According to recent reports, as he said, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

According to recent reports, then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

“The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he said in a statement at the time.

McDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

“Jim McDermott was as substantial as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”.

#157478. Birdsong has more in common with human speech than scientists expected

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1030 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Birdsong has more in common with human speech than scientists expected

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1030 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A comparison of 367 bird species and 52 human languages reveals unexpected similarities in the rhythms and patterns of vocal communication.
  • Birds and humans share some surprisingly similar patterns when they make sounds.
  • The finding comes from a comparison of the songs of 367 bird species with people speaking and singing in 52 languages.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A comparison of 367 bird species and 52 human languages reveals unexpected similarities in the rhythms and patterns of vocal communication.

Birds and humans share some surprisingly similar patterns when they make sounds. Even birds that never learn their songs naturally produce rhythms much like those found in human speech and music.

The finding comes from a comparison of the songs of 367 bird species with people speaking and singing in 52 languages.

Three patterns of human speech and music appeared across the birds, in those that learn their songs and in those that don’t.

The authors interpret that as a sign that the patterns come from the shared mechanics of making sound rather than from learning alone.

Logan James of McGill University and the University of Texas at Austin led the work with Jon Sakata of McGill. Several co-authors work at McGill’s Centre for Research on Brain, Language and Music.

In an interview with Earth.com, James noted that the shared patterns were what excited the team most.

“These results highlight that, despite the tremendous diversity across human languages and hundreds of species of birds, there are still fundamental shared sequencing patterns,” he noted.

The recordings came from xeno-canto, where birders around the world upload recordings. The team kept only recordings the recordist had rated top quality and labeled as song rather than calls.

No second species could be in the background, no playback could have been used to provoke the bird, and the singer had to have been seen.

In a recent development, software then split each song into its separate sounds, and experienced annotators checked every sound. That work produced more than 74,500 individual sounds from about 5,900 songs.

The researchers paired each group of vocal learners with closely related birds that do not learn their songs: songbirds with suboscines, and hummingbirds with nightjars.

On the human side, the team used recordings of people speaking and singing in 52 languages, made for an earlier project.

According to recent reports, in human speech and song, the pitch rarely leaps far from one syllable to the next. The team measured the pitch at the end of each bird sound and the start of the next.

Across the birds, the jumps were smaller than chance would produce.

Human voices also keep a beat, with sounds spaced evenly in time.

Birdsong revealed the same pattern more often than would be expected by chance.

And people generally stretch the last sound of a phrase, the way a singer holds a final note.

Birds did that too. Their songs also tended to grow louder through the middle of a phrase and fade at the end, as human music does.

Industry observers note that songbirds have been the usual comparison for human speech because they, like us, learn their songs by listening. This study could set them against close relatives that don’t.

Sakata told Earth.com that the team expected birds that learn their songs to show greater similarities to human speech, since people also learn to speak.

“What surprised us was that the songs of birds that do not learn their songs (e.g., suboscines, nightjars) actually had comparable patterns to us relative to the vocal-learning birds,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that where vocal learning did make a difference, it did not act the same way in songbirds as in hummingbirds. The authors counted that as no consistent effect.

Sources indicate that the matches were not perfect. Unlike human voices, which tended to become quieter throughout a phrase, birdsong tended to grow louder in the middle before fading at the end.

The authors suspect breathing explains part of it.

A person usually speaks or sings a whole phrase on one breath, and they suggest that is why the volume drops toward the end. Birds take tiny breaths between the sounds in a song.

Industry observers note that lung size may matter too. Across the birds, bigger species stretched their final sounds more, and a human has much bigger lungs than any of them.

But nightjars, among the largest birds in the study, stretched their final sounds even more than people do, so size can’t explain all of it.

The team also ran a broader measurement of how pitch and rhythm change together across a whole phrase, the same one that separates speech from song in human recordings.

By that measure, bird songs as a group were closer to human speech than to human singing. Hummingbirds and suboscines came out nearest to both, closer than the songbirds.

James said no large group of birds was closest to human patterns overall.

A few species were, on that combined measure, among them the scaled antbird, the blackhead antbird and the rufous-tailed hummingbird.

Songbirds and suboscines did keep a steadier beat than hummingbirds and nightjars, so they are the better birds to study for the roots of human rhythm.

In a commentary published alongside the study, Kazuo Okanoya of Teikyo University wrote that the work gives researchers a basis for testing the mechanisms behind the shared patterns.

“Linguistic concepts can guide such tests but should not be used in place of experimental data,” he added.

The study was based entirely on recordings, so the researchers could not confirm whether similarities in how birds and humans produce sound explain the shared patterns.

It also remains unclear whether listeners’ preferences help shape these patterns.

Sakata noted very little is known about the shape of the voice box in many of these species, and that mapping that variety is a next step.

James said earlier work by the group found that people tend to like the same male courtship sounds that females of that species like.

“So we are also curious to examine how much birds (and humans) like the sound of patterns that conform to these universal patterns,” James said.

Other features of human music, such as distinct notes and nested layers of structure, have not been checked in birds yet. The authors wrote that those are the next measurements to take.

The full study was published in the journal Science.
