📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve got a dead car battery, you’ll want the option to revive it without waiting for help. According to AAA’s most recent report, of the 27 million calls received across the country for roadside assistance, 7 million of those vehicles had battery trouble. The causes may include anything from neglecting to turn off your car’s ignition or headlights, residing in an extremely cold climate, or even a slowly deteriorating alternator.

A portable jump starter, which is a compact and powerful battery consisting of lightweight lithium-ion, is a handy device that’s faster, safer, and more convenient than jumper cables because you don’t need to find another car with a willing driver.

It has been revealed that like all batteries, lithium-ion cells have different power ratings and can become depleted from repeated use or by sitting idle over time. That’s why before purchasing a portable jump starter, consider these two specs: peak amperage (amps) which conveys how much power a device can deliver, and capacity (rated in milliampere-hours, mAh), indicating how long a device can hold a charge when stored and still have enough power to provide a jump. It’s also vital to monitor the charge level on your portable jump starter from time to time. I do this regularly while waiting to fill my gas tank.

Recent findings suggest that there are other convenience features these devices offer, like USB ports to recharge portable electronics and lights for illumination when it’s dark. Many portable jump starters have what’s called a boost button, which I recommend having, as it supplies extra momentary power for severely drained batteries. After several rounds of testing, research, and evaluation, these are the top portable jump starters to buy now.

I’ve owned close to a dozen vehicles during my 30-year-plus career writing about cars and have had plenty of dead batteries. I keep jumper cables in each of my three current vehicles, and now I also have a portable jump starter on board along with a portable tire inflator, dash cam, and Cobra RAD 700i radar detector, which I move between vehicles depending on which I decide to drive.

Recent findings suggest that in short, each device in this roundup can promptly start a vehicle with a depleted battery. While testing each product, I also evaluated its peak instantaneous power measured in amps, power capacity measured in milliampere-hours, the quantity and variety of output ports to charge portable electronics, and extras such as lights and a boost button.

My recommendations are based on a product’s price, capability, and capacity to fit a wide array of vehicles and budgets. I took into account my own experiences with portable jump starters, each brand’s reputation, and for further background, I spoke with fellow car enthusiasts and auto journalists to get their impressions.

Industry observers note that with 6,000-amp peak current to jump-start a vehicle with up to a 12.0-liter diesel engine coupled with 27,000 mAh of power capacity, the Gooloo GT6000 is the most powerful device in our guide. The GT6000 offers up to 24 months of standby time—and with that, you get incredible peace of mind. This device can sit unused for long stretches and still be counted on to crank your car when needed. If its battery is depleted, the GT6000 is ready to jump-start a vehicle after just 7 minutes of recharging and is fully recharged in 1.4 hours via its 100-watt USB-C in/out port.

According to recent reports, this device also stands out for its generous quantity and variety of charging ports. In addition to a 100-watt USB-C in/out port, it also has a 12-volt/cigarette-lighter cord to recharge its battery in a pinch. A 15 volt/10-amp DC port can be used to power assorted car accessories like portable air pumps and power inverters. There are two USB-A power ports, one rated at 5-volts/2.4-amps and another rated for 5/9/12-volts.

According to recent reports, the GT6000 is one of only two devices here with an LCD screen, which makes checking battery level, charging output, temperature, and jump-start status quick and easy. There are 10 safety features, in addition to a built-in LED flashlight with three lighting modes (flashlight, strobe, and SOS) that provides illumination when using the device in low-light situations—important so other motorists can see you if you’re stuck on the side of the road.

While the GT6000 admittedly provides more power than most motorists will likely need, and it’s one of the heaviest of our picks, it is without question the best overall jump starter for maximum instantaneous power, long standby time, quick recharging, and plenty of output ports.

The AstroAI S8 isn’t the most powerful jump-starter recommended but it’s one of the lowest-priced and is user friendly and small enough to fit in your car’s glove box or map pocket. Although it taps out on vehicles with anything larger than a 6.0-liter gas or 3.0-liter diesel engine, it’s fine for most vehicles. I’ve kept this in one of my vehicles for months and used it several times to provide jump-starts to others without an issue.

Industry observers note that protection against reverse polarity, overcurrent, overvoltage, overload, overcharge, over discharge, and short circuiting are built in. The AstroAI S8 has two 5-volt/2.4-amp USB-A output ports to charge portable devices and an LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes. It is supplied with a USB A to USB C charging cable to recharge the device.

Sources indicate that the interface is one of the most barebones of all the units tested—just a power button and four blue LEDs to indicate power level. It does have a boost button but is the only unit of our selections without a shut-off switch; instead it automatically powers off after 30 seconds.Full AstroAI S8 Portable Jump Starter Review.

Industry observers note that this is the smallest device I tested (only slightly larger than most smartphones) and the lightest at 1.2 pounds. With 2,000 amps of peak power, the Gooloo GP2000 can jump-start vehicles with up to 8.0-liter gas or 6.0-liter diesel engines and its 12,000 mAh of capacity is impressive for its size and price.

According to recent reports, it has 10 safety protection features including short circuit and reverse polarity, and a 400-lumen LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes to provide light in dark environments and during emergency roadside stops. It comes with two USB-A outputs—one 5/9/12-volt and one 5-volt/2.4-amp—for charging portable devices, a USB-C charging cable, and a storage case instead of a bag like many portable jump starters at this price.

Like the AstroAI S8, it has only an on-off button. It’s easy to use and has a boost button. I recommend this option for anyone looking for a small, inexpensive, and hassle-free portable jump starter.

With an IP65 water-resistance rating and rubberized casing, the Noco Boost Plus is the portable jump starter I turn to during the rainy season in Oregon—which means anytime other than summer. I go for this one because it has spark-proof and reverse polarity protection for safe use in wet or dry conditions.

Its 1,000-amp peak power rating can start vehicles with up to 6.0-liter gas and 3.0-liter diesel engines. However, its 2,150 mAh capacity is the lowest of any product here, so it may not hold a charge as long as jump starters with a higher capacity. While this is adequate, I don’t recommend a mAh rating any lower.

Recent findings suggest that the Noco GB40’s 100-lumen flashlight is dimmer than that of some of the other units in this roundup but it has the most modes, six total, which include 100-, 50-, and 10 percent; blink, SOS, and strobe. It also comes with a 1-foot USB-C charging cable, but it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A output port for charging your portable electronics.

Full Noco GB40 Boost Plus Review.

If you own a large vehicle, the Noco Boost X GBX155 cranks out 4,250 amps to boost batteries instantaneously for vehicles with up to 10.0-liter gas and 8.0-liter diesel engines, and has an impressive 26,750 mAh capacity, just shy of the Gooloo GT6000’s 27,000-mAh spec. A 60-watt USB-C input/output allows recharging from 0-to-100 percent capacity in 2.7 hours to ensure it’s ready to jump-start a vehicle after charging only 5 minutes (slightly faster than the Gooloo GT6000’s 7 minutes.).

I found the Noco Boost X GBX155 more complicated to operate than the other portable jump starters I tested. For example, it doesn’t have a boost button like other units but rather a manual override feature that’s used to jump start severely depleted batteries if the device detects the battery is below 3 volts. Aactivating the feature requires holding the Manual Override button for 3 seconds, which can send the GBX155’s maximum output of 4,250 amps to jump start a vehicle. This Manual Override shuts off the Noco’s automatic spark-proof and reverse-polarity protection so users need to be extra careful to attach the jumper cables correctly (red to positive, black to negative) to avoid damaging the car’s electrical system, and not touch the clamps together, which can create dangerous sparking.

The Noco is heavy, too, at 5.8 pounds. In addition to its 60-watt USB-C input/output, it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A port whereas other lower-priced devices have at least two. But you won’t be working in the dark if you are trying to start your battery at night. This device has a 500-lumen LED flashlight that’s the brightest of the portable jump starters in our roundup. Another perk: it’s got an IP65 waterproof rating (with its input/output ports covered) that only the Gooloo GT6000 and Noco GB40 also have.

It has been revealed that for motorheads with multiple vehicles and a garage or shop to keep them, the Clore Automotive Jump-N-Carry JNC660 is a worthy device to have on hand. Its 120-volt male receptacle connects to an extension cord so that it can be powered by a regular wall outlet and is always charged and ready.

Recent findings suggest that this device uses a lead-acid battery instead of a lithium-ion one. This makes the battery replaceable, so this device is not ultimately disposable like portable jump starters with a lithium-ion battery. At 18 pounds, it’s by far the heaviest here, but also has the longest (46 inches) and thickest (2-gauge) jumper cables.

With 1,700 peak amps, it’s not the most powerful portable jump starter included but makes up for that with a 22,000 mAh rating which means its internal battery holds a charge longer. A built-in digital voltmeter shows the battery’s state of charge before and after a jump start and it has a DC outlet to power 12-volt accessories such as a tire inflator or power inverter. A notable drawback: It doesn’t have USB output ports.

For years, I relied on a Battery Tender trickle charger to supply a slow, steady current to keep the battery in my classic Chevy Impala SS charged. If you also have a vehicle that sits idle for months on end, check out the Battery Tender Charge N Start 4120. It does double duty as a trickle charger and a jump starter. However, combining two devices in one comes with compromises such as not having output ports to charge portable devices, or a boost button.

According to recent reports, with 1,200 amps of instantaneous current, this device can jump start cars with up to 6.0-liter gas or 4.0-liter diesel engines and proficiently cranked the engine on several large and small vehicles during my testing. Its basic push-button interface makes the Charge N Start a breeze to operate. Safety features include spark-proof connection, reverse-polarity protection, and more.

This portable jump starter sends a small amount of current to traditional lead-acid as well as lithium batteries at 4 amps, and an onboard microprocessor maintains the optimal voltage to keep a battery at 100-percent capacity without overcharging during long-term storage. It also includes temperature compensation to handle a range of climates.

It has been revealed that something you may need to think about is its size. Its larger than other trickle chargers I’ve used, which affects placement. Ideally, a trickle charger should be located close to the battery under a car’s hood. The Charge N Start may be too large to tuck away under the closed hood of certain vehicles, but a supplied 6-foot extension cable that attaches to low-profile battery-charging clamps allows locating the device away from the engine on, say, a shelf next to a wall outlet.

The Noco AX65 is another portable jump starter we’ve tested and recommend, but we moved it out of our guide because it’s not singularly a portable jump starter like the others. This is a combo device with a portable air compressor so you can start dead batteries and inflate flat tires. What I like is that the unit doesn’t skimp on either function. The jump starter has an impressive 16,000 mAh capacity and delivers 2,000 amps of peak power while the tire inflator pumps out 67 liters per minute of airflow, which converts to 2.3 cubic feet per minute (cfm)—well above average for the portable tire inflators I’ve tested.

The portable jump starter can crank a dead battery on vehicles with gas engines as large as 8.0 liters and diesel engines up to 6.0 liters. It can be used for SUVs, boats, and snowmobiles. The not-so-good news: It’s short on output ports compared to the other portable jump starters here, and heavy at more than 9 pounds.

In a recent development, portable jump starters are essentially heavy-duty batteries that come with jumper cables, controls, and accessories like lights, charging ports, and air pumps. Here’s what to look for when shopping for a portable jump starter that fits your vehicle, needs, and budget.

Sources indicate that the two most important specs to look for when comparing portable jump starters are peak amperes (amps) and milliampere-hours (mAh). Peak amps indicate the maximum short-term current a device can deliver, while mAh measures how much electrical charge a battery can store.

Bigger is better for both specs, although mAh isn’t always as prominent or even stated with portable jump starters compared to peak amps. About 400 to 600 peak amps is sufficient to jump-start vehicles like cars and crossovers, although large SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles may require up to 1,500 or 2,000 amps. Some portable jump starters come with a boost button that provides roughly 10 additional amps and is helpful when reviving a very dead battery that needs an extra jolt of juice. At least 10,000 mAh of capacity means the battery in a portable jump starter will hold enough charge for 3 to 6 months to deliver 5 to 10 jump-starts.

Portable jump starters are a much safer alternative to using jumper cables to revive a dead battery because connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that can sometimes ignite gas produced by the battery and cause an explosion. Also, if you connect the cables incorrectly, called reverse polarity, it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, portable jump starters have built-in protection against issues like sparking and reverse polarity in addition to other safety features and are much less risky and easier to use.

Industry observers note that most portable jump starters also come in handy for recharging phones, tablets, and other portable devices. USB output ports are the most common, but a few devices also provide a 12-volt outlet. While USB ports typically charge at 2.5 to 5 volts, a 12-volt outlet can not only charge a device faster but can also be used to power devices such as portable air pumps and coolers.

If you need to jump-start a vehicle at night, you’ll be thankful your portable jump starter has an LED flashlight. Typically a portable jump starter’s lighting feature also provides strobe or SOS patterns to warn other motorists on the road of your presence.

In a recent development, look for a portable jump starter with a boost button to give an extra jolt of juice to a very depleted battery when the device’s standard output can’t crank the engine. This surge of power gives you about 15 to 30 seconds to start the car once the boost button is pressed.

In a recent development, A portable jump starter rated for 400 to 600 amps is sufficient to jump-start most passenger vehicles such as cars, crossovers, and smaller SUVs. But for larger SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles you want to look for a device with at least 1,500 to 2,000 amps. Weather also affects a car battery and engine, so if you live in a very cold climate more power may be needed to jump-start a low or dead battery.

In a recent development, yes and no since it depends on the wide range of passenger vehicles available. A portable jump starter with a lower amp rating can jump-start smaller vehicles such as most cars, crossovers, and small SUVs. But a large SUV or truck with a large engine will require a portable jump starter with a higher amp rating.

Peak power rating (measured in amps) to ensure a portable jump starter has enough juice to crank your vehicle and capacity (measured in milliamp hours) that indicates how long it can potentially hold a charge are the most two important. Other features to look for include the number and types of output charging ports, whether it has a 12-volt output and charging input, a boost button, and a flashlight.

According to recent reports, definitely. Make sure to first read the owner’s manual to understand how your portable jump starter works before connecting it to a car’s battery. When using it, take off any jewelry and wear safety glasses and gloves anytime you work on a vehicle and especially around a battery. Most portable jump starters come with built-in safety features that will concern a warning if they are connected incorrectly. But it’s up to you to double-check that the jump starter’s red/positive and black/negative clamps are connected to the (typically) red positive and black negative terminals of the car battery.

Yes, a portable jump starter is a much safer alternative to using traditional jumper cables to start a vehicle with a dead battery. Connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that have the potential to ignite gas produced by a battery which in some instances can lead to an explosion. And if you connect the cables incorrectly (in reverse polarity) it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, most portable jump starters come with built-in protection against challenges like sparking and reverse polarity and are much less risky and easier to use. Plus, with a portable jump starter you don’t have to find another car—and a driver—like you do with jump cables. That said, I carry a set of jumper cables as a backup.

#157476. Premature birth may change the brain’s biological clock

Premature birth may change the brain’s biological clock

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brain scans and donated tissue show that premature birth sets the cerebellum on its own track, leaving it out of step at the due date.
  • Premature birth interrupts a critical period of brain development.
  • Now, researchers have found that even by their original due dates, babies born prematurely show signs of altered development in a key region of the brain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brain scans and donated tissue show that premature birth sets the cerebellum on its own track, leaving it out of step at the due date.

Premature birth interrupts a critical period of brain development.

Now, researchers have found that even by their original due dates, babies born prematurely show signs of altered development in a key region of the brain.

Sources indicate that the cerebellum of a baby born early matures on a different track. At the due date, its cells are in a different state from a full-term baby’s, according to a new study of brain scans, developmental checkups and donated tissue.

Georgios Sanidas and Gabriele Simonti of Children’s National Hospital in Washington, D.C., led the work.

The study’s senior authors were Panagiotis Kratimenos of Children’s National and the George Washington University School of Medicine and Vittorio Gallo of Seattle Children’s Research Institute.

The tissue came from infants who had died and whose families consented to autopsy, and the authors thank those families in the paper.

In an interview with Earth.com, Kratimenos noted that the work offers parents of preterm babies relief as well as hope.

“Our work highlights that premature birth does not break the brain, nor does it simply pause it,” Kratimenos stated.

Between 24 and 40 weeks of pregnancy, the cerebellum grows about fivefold in volume, faster than any other part of the brain.

It handles movement and balance, and it is wired into thinking and language as well.

For a baby born at 26 weeks, much of that growth takes place in a neonatal intensive care unit.

Doctors have known that early birth changes how the cerebellum grows and how a child develops.

What they didn’t know was what happens to the cells inside it, because that can only be studied in human tissue.

The team followed 176 infants born early, none of whom had major brain injury, through scans and checkups.

At the due date, each extra week of pregnancy before birth was worth about 230 cubic millimeters of cerebellum, in proportion to the rest of the brain.

Recent findings suggest that ultrasound revealed the size gap already in place at 28 weeks. The babies born earliest then grew at the same rate as the rest, so they had not closed it by the due date.

Later checkups demonstrated the same pattern. Between nine months and three years of age, the babies born at the lowest gestational ages were more likely to have motor, thinking and language delays.

A smaller cerebellum went with motor and thinking delays in particular. Lung disease and the other complications of intensive care shaped the numbers, but they didn’t explain them.

To see the cells, the team turned to cerebellar tissue from 83 infants who had died, born anywhere from very early to full term. In 11 of them, the researchers mapped which genes were switched on where.

Three patterns of gene activity tracked how early a baby had been born.

The cerebellum’s most numerous neurons, the small granule cells, were still running an immature program in the babies born earliest.

In babies born closer to term, that program had given way to one built for forming and firing connections.

Under a standard microscope, the granule cells in the earliest-born babies look finished, because they have already reached their adult position.

“Even though those granule cells had reached the right neighborhood, they were still carrying the genetic features of immature cells,” Gallo noted.

The large neurons that carry the cerebellum’s output, the Purkinje cells, were different again.

In the earliest-born infants their genes were tuned to building cell material, with signs of stress, rather than to settling into a mature circuit.

“Being born early forces those same cells to prioritize immediate survival over wiring, leaving them in an unfinished state even months later,” Kratimenos told Earth.com.

Under the microscope, in 77 of the brains, the differences were structural too. A temporary outer layer of brain cell precursors that normally disappears after birth lingered longer in preterm infants.

In full-term infants the density of Purkinje cells fell with age, the normal trimming that refines a circuit. In preterm infants it stayed flat.

The layer that holds the Purkinje cells’ branches grew at the same rate in both groups.

The preterm cerebellum continued to grow without showing the same signs of cellular maturation.

It kept its overall architecture while its development went a different way, which is why a scan that measures size alone may miss it.

According to recent reports, preterm babies are assessed, monitored and enrolled in trials by postmenstrual age, the weeks since the mother’s last period. The authors argue that this number measures time, not biological maturity.

Two babies at the same postmenstrual age can be at different developmental stages.

Treatments given around a premature birth, such as magnesium sulfate before delivery and caffeine after it, may therefore act on tissue that differs from one baby to the next.

“To time treatments properly, we have to match our therapies to the biological clock of a baby’s brain cells, rather than their age on the calendar,” Gallo noted.

Gallo suggests that therapies designed to promote brain wiring may be less effective before the cells reach the appropriate stage of development.

In a commentary on the paper, Molly Kelly-Goss and Elizabeth Crouch wrote that a preterm infant may follow two calendars.

One is the cerebellum’s physical growth, and the other is the maturation of its cells and molecules.

In their words, “neither captures the true complexity of brain health at the time, nor what it means for the child years later.”.

According to recent reports, the study can’t separate the timing of birth from everything that comes with it. Inflammation, low oxygen and the stress of life outside the womb all arrive together.

The tissue and the scans also came from different infants, since the cerebellum can’t be sampled in a living baby’s brain, and each infant had one MRI scan.

Whether the gap persists, shrinks or is made up later in childhood is not known.

The authors wrote that the same slow maturation that leaves the preterm cerebellum vulnerable may also leave its development open to change for longer.

Gallo said the team’s gene signatures for each stage could guide treatment in two steps.

The first would protect a baby from inflammation and stress in intensive care, and the second would bring in therapies that boost brain wiring once the cells are ready.

Testing that will take studies that time treatments to a baby’s biological stage.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

Power shutoffs meant to prevent wildfires may carry unexpected health risks

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Planned power shutoffs in California were linked to more respiratory-related hospital visits, particularly when wildfire smoke was also present.
  • When the wind picks up on a hot, dry day in fire country, the power company may switch off the electricity on purpose.
  • It has been revealed that A planned shutoff has a cost of its own, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Planned power shutoffs in California were linked to more respiratory-related hospital visits, particularly when wildfire smoke was also present.

When the wind picks up on a hot, dry day in fire country, the power company may switch off the electricity on purpose. A line with no current in it can’t start a fire when it drops into dry brush.

It has been revealed that A planned shutoff has a cost of its own, though. In California, on days when a large shutoff reached a neighborhood, people there were more likely to turn up at an emergency room with a breathing problem.

The rise was largest among people with chronic lung disease, and wildfire smoke in the air at the same time made it larger still.

Lauren Blair Wilner, an epidemiologist at the University of Washington, led the analysis with colleagues at Scripps Institution of Oceanography and Columbia University.

Utilities call these planned outages public safety power shutoffs, or PSPS, and no study before this one had measured what they do to hospital traffic.

In an interview with Earth.com, Wilner pointed to the days when the two overlapped.

“Surprisingly, the effects of a PSPS event and wildfire smoke co-occurring were not simply additive – we found evidence that their effects on health were multiplicative,” she said.

Three major California utilities serve 88% of the state’s electric customers. They have run these power shutoffs since 2012 and report each one to the California Public Utilities Commission.

The research group PSE Healthy Energy compiled those reports.

Wilner’s team matched the reports for 2013 through 2019, by zip code, against every emergency room visit and unplanned hospital admission by adults across 1,504 California zip codes.

Those records came from the California Department of Health Care Access and Information and included more than 6.6 million visits for breathing problems.

Each visit day was compared with the other days of the same weekday that month, so every patient served as their own comparison.

A large shutoff meant more than 593 customers in a zip code without power.

In a recent development, on those days, the odds of an emergency room visit or admission for a breathing problem were about 6% higher. Smaller power shutoffs made no measurable difference.

Shutoffs and smoke arrive together more often than not. Of the 11,293 zip-code days with a shutoff, 7,656 also had wildfire smoke in the air.

Industry observers note that asked by Earth.com what else the study highlighted, Wilner came back to those overlapping days. “Co-occurrence is what we really need to think about here,” she said.

Because days with both outnumbered days with a shutoff alone, she added, shutoffs should be studied together with the fires they are meant to prevent.

According to recent reports, picture a day with a large shutoff and 10 micrograms of smoke particles in each cubic meter of air. The odds of a breathing-related visit that day were 16% higher than on a day with neither.

The shutoff alone added about 6% and that much smoke alone about 1%, so the pair did more than add up.

The pattern was strongest among people with COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a long-term illness that narrows the airways and makes breathing hard work.

It has been revealed that on days with a large shutoff, the odds of a COPD visit were 29% higher. With smoke on top, they were 37% higher.

Many people with COPD rely on an oxygen concentrator, a machine that pulls oxygen out of room air.

It has been revealed that it runs on electricity, and its battery typically lasts three to four hours. A typical shutoff in this study lasted 86 hours, more than three days.

Wilner said planners should take simultaneous outages into account as they prepare for wildfires and expand healthcare capacity.

“It is essential to put measures in place to ensure that people relying on electricity dependent medical equipment have access to power and can readily access healthcare, if needed,” she said.

Visits for heart problems didn’t rise during shutoffs, with or without smoke, and neither did visits for mental health crises.

Earlier studies of blackouts in Upcoming York State and Florida largely agree, suggesting that outages may be more strongly associated with respiratory problems than heart problems.

How long a shutoff lasted also mattered less than how many people it reached.

When the team counted total hours without power over the previous week instead, they found no link between duration alone and hospital visits.

Sources indicate that each additional 1,000 customers without power, on the other hand, was linked to about 2% higher odds of a breathing-related visit. For COPD visits, the figure was 6%.

Utilities report outages by circuit, so the team can’t say who inside a zip code lost power.

The researchers assumed customers were spread evenly along each circuit, which means some people counted as exposed weren’t.

Industry observers note that nor can the records show whether a patient was home during a shutoff. People may travel to a place that still has power, and breathe more smoke on the way.

Only adults 20 and older who reached a hospital are counted, so anyone who got sick at home and stayed there is missing.

The study covered 2013 to 2019, when planned power shutoffs were less common than they are today.

Industry observers note that since 2022, utilities in Washington, Oregon, Idaho, and Hawaii have used shutoffs too. California requires utilities to warn customers first and to open centers where people can charge devices.

Wilner’s team didn’t test whether those centers keep anyone out of the emergency room.

Wilner’s team is turning to what happens after a wildfire or other disaster, when outages and evacuations overlap.

“There are not complete datasets on historical evacuations and power outages after disasters, making it impossible to study the ways in which these things play out and affect health after an event,” she told Earth.com.

Those records, she said, would show what affected communities need and how to reach them.

For now, seven years of California records offer valuable insight into the potential health consequences of planned power shutoffs.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Medicine.

Industry News: The 7 Best Pocket Knives for Everyday Tasks and Outdoor Adventures

📅 07 Aug 2017 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4045 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Cutting tools were likely some of the earliest tools fashioned by our prehistoric ancestors, so it’s perhaps surprising that knives are still one of the most popular tools in an age of 3D printers and electric scooters.
  • Modern EDC pocket knives have evolved quite a way beyond stone shards, with a bewildering variety of blade steels, blade shapes, opening and locking mechanisms as well as diverse aesthetics ranging from tactical to minimalist to outdoorsy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Cutting tools were likely some of the earliest tools fashioned by our prehistoric ancestors, so it’s perhaps surprising that knives are still one of the most popular tools in an age of 3D printers and electric scooters.

Modern EDC pocket knives have evolved quite a way beyond stone shards, with a bewildering variety of blade steels, blade shapes, opening and locking mechanisms as well as diverse aesthetics ranging from tactical to minimalist to outdoorsy.

It has been revealed that this guide focuses on functional folding knives with (mostly) approachable price tags that you’ll want to use every day, not place under glass. I test dozens of knives each year, and I’ve chosen my favorites below only from the knives I’ve personally used.

Recent findings suggest that the Iridium is one of Kershaw’s most popular releases and for good reason. It’s priced modestly with a secure bar lock-out, easy one-handed opening and closing, and it just looks cool. It’s also the sweet spot for most people in terms of size, weight, and style. Not ultralight (just over three ounces), the 6061-T6’s aluminum handle and slim profile keep it barely noticeable in your pocket.

Industry observers note that when testing, I found the 4.5-inch length was great for my medium-sized hands and shouldn’t be too big or small for any hands—or jobs. Kershaw offers low- and mid-priced production knives made in China, but they follow up with high-quality control in their Oregon facilities and consistently deliver designs that just work.

At the core of the Iridium series is a secure, Benchmade-style crossbar lock, and while there are models that veer into Benchmade prices, many models, including the original, can be had for less than $100.

Industry observers note that the Iridium is easy to use—opening with a smooth action, activated by the thumb stud opener. Though it’s not spring-assisted, the blade flicks open fast without resistance. Closing is similarly smooth—just pull down on the crossbar lock and close with a finger, or hold upright and let the blade fall shut. I usually prefer the satisfying speed of a flipper, but the smooth action of the Iridium’s thumb stud opening rivals the Benchmade Bugout’s, and it quickly grew on me.

Recent findings suggest that the D2 steel used in the original, which offers decent edge retention and durability, is common in lower-cost knives but can rust if you abuse it. A compromise option: Go with the black oxide-coated D2 blade which keeps all but the cutting edge sealed off from rust. The look on all these versions of the Iridium matches the modern design features, and the only drawback of how smooth and slick the knife looks is that it’s not the best for operating in wet or muddy conditions where grip could become an matter.

Full Kershaw Iridium Pocket Knife Review.

Coast is one of several Oregon-based knife manufacturers (the tech giant also sells a wide range of flashlights and headlamps) to offer a range of budget-friendly folding pocket knives. My favorite from their lineup is the fairly small but robust Contra, which has an all-metal build and a lifetime warranty despite the low cost. The wharncliffe blade, made from a softer 7CR17 steel, dulls faster than high-end steels but has the benefit of being easy to sharpen at home.

The wharncliffe blade gives you the utility of a box cutter blade but much more versatility as you retain a decent point for puncturing tasks, and I’ve come to prefer it for everyday carry over more traditional drop point shapes. Coast adds durability to its budget steel with a black oxide coating that I found doesn’t scratch easily. The knife is a full stainless-steel build with a good-looking stonewash finish on the handle which integrates the frame lock system.

The flipper opening is fast and satisfying for knife fidgeters but it’s usually safer to employ a two-handed closure. Given the overseas production and ultra-low sticker price, this pocket knife’s durability could be a potential concern, but I’ve used mine roughly near-daily for more than a year and haven’t broken or chipped the blade. It still looks new.

Benchmade is an American knife brand based in Oregon with a loyal following for its premium production pocket knives. Known for lightweight designs, modern materials, and innovation, the brand has produced many favorites—but my top pick is the Benchmade 535 Bugout.

According to recent reports, to me, the Bugout captures what Benchmade does best: an ultralight folder that’s still strong, well-built, and made with high-quality steel (and the same holds true with the Benchmade 533 Mini Bugout). Some might argue the Benchmade Osborne 940 is the brand’s most iconic knife, but I reach for the Bugout every time—especially for hunting, camping, backpacking, or backcountry skiing, where weight matters.

The design is modern without feeling overly tactical. It’s streamlined with a simple profile and a practical drop-point blade. The textured Grivory scales—glass-reinforced plastic—keep weight incredibly low while maintaining rigidity.

Sources indicate that at under two ounces and just 0.42 inches thick, the Bugout is barely noticeable in a pocket, making it ideal for long outdoor trips. For those who don’t like the Grivory feel, there are versions with aluminum or carbon-fiber scales and a range of steel options.

Operation is another highlight. Benchmade’s Axis Lock uses a spring-loaded crossbar that allows easy one-handed opening and closing from either hand while keeping fingers out of the blade path. The mechanism is simple, strong, and easy to maintain—I even built one myself at the Benchmade factory and found it intuitive without instructions.

In terms of cutting performance, my Bugouts arrived razor-sharp out of the box. I prefer the standard S30V steel because it balances edge retention with easier sharpening in the field, though higher-end options like S90V are available if you want longer-lasting sharpness. S30V is also tough and corrosion-resistant, which suits hard outdoor use.

In a recent development, benchmade’s lifetime warranty and sharpening service add real long-term value. The Bugout isn’t cheap, but with its reliability, ultralight design, and customization options, it’s easy to recommend—especially for outdoor enthusiasts or anyone wanting a high-quality everyday carry knife.

Full Benchmade Bugout 535 Review.

Case is one of the original American knife brands still standing and, unlike many of their competitors that have shipped production to China, most of Case’s knives are still designed and produced in Bradford, Pennsylvania.

Whether or not that matters to you, Case makes great knives, and while they sell a lot of nostalgic designs unchanged for a century, the Kinzua is one of their modern EDC offerings that departs from the Case aesthetic with an all-metal build, flipper action, sharp lines, and a tanto blade.

According to recent reports, the satin-finished S35VN steel blade is a good compromise of hardness and edge durability while still being fairly easy to sharpen at home. It also has a lightly weathered look that should hide abuse well. One note is that, while extremely sturdy, the all-metal frame-lock design is pretty stiff to close out of the box.

Recent findings suggest that releasing the frame lock requires some force and closing requires a few moves. With a little practice I was able to comfortably operate it one-handed, but folks with smaller or weaker hands may not feel the same.

It has been revealed that the Bugout is one of our favorite Benchmade folders, and we recommend it above as our Best Lightweight pocket knife. But the brand’s new Bugout Vapyr variant is different enough to warrant its own place on the podium. The most noticeable difference is the width. The original Bugout is featherlight at two ounces, but the Vapyr gets that down to 1.72 ounces and shrinks the width by 3 mm, which is very obvious in the hand.

It has been revealed that it’s impressive engineering, but practically, it takes a knife that was barely noticeable in the pocket and makes it borderline undetectable. It costs $375—nearly double the regular Bugout—so this is for folks with fewer budget constraints who are willing to spend for the lightest, thinnest folder that doesn’t compromise on utility and durability.

It has been revealed that part of that price jump can be chalked up to Benchmade swapping in MagnaCut steel for the S30V in the baseline Bugout. S30V is already a great blade steel with high corrosion resistance and incredible edge retention, and Benchmade has come to be known for using it. But MagnaCut is a step above on both metrics.

Industry observers note that the other big change is the Axis lock, which remains functionally the same but swaps in a new stepped slide in place of the longstanding metal button. It’s a minor swap that first-time Benchmade buyers likely won’t even notice. But having used Axis locks for years, I much prefer the new slide.

It has been revealed that there’s a subtle internal change from an omega spring to a tension spring. It didn’t feel different when I used it side by side with the original Bugout, but Benchmade says the tension springs have a longer lifespan. It’s worth noting that while better durability is welcome considering the price tag, all Benchmade knives have a lifetime warranty (and lifetime sharpening service) if a spring were to fail.

One drawback from the original Bugout is that, at least with the Bugout Vapyr I tested, the pivot is much tighter and requires more force to open. You can open a Bugout one of two ways. One, you can use the thumb stud to spin the blade out into the locked-open position. Alternatively, you can pull the Axis lock open and flick the blade open. This second option requires a touch of timing and gets harder with the Vapyr’s tighter pivot, though I didn’t find the thumb stud actuation any more challenging in the Vapyr.

Full Benchmade Bugout Vapyr Review.

In a recent development, I’ve been looking for a good automatic pocket knife for years, and the CRKT Twist Tighe Automatic is the only one that I’ve found that doesn't feel like a novelty knife. It’s compact, lightweight, fun to use, and practical enough for everyday carry while still delivering the fun factor that draws many people to automatic knives in the first place.

Automatics, often called switchblades, are popular with knife enthusiasts because they’re inherently fidget-friendly. The Twist Tighe is an out-the-front (OTF) automatic, meaning the blade deploys straight out of the front of the handle. Besides being undeniably cool, I find the operation safer than many folding knives because it’s harder to accidentally place your fingers in the blade’s path when opening and closing.

The highlight is its smooth double-action mechanism. Sliding the spine button forward fires the blade; pulling it back retracts it. Many automatics I’ve tried are either stiff or inconsistent, but the Twist Tighe feels smooth and reliable even after repeated use. That ease of operation also makes it surprisingly approachable for people who aren’t experienced with knives.

Sources indicate that the design comes from Canadian knife designer Brian Tighe, and the handle’s raised spiral grooves are a distinctive touch fans of his work will recognize. In the all-black configuration, the knife looks sleek and slightly dramatic without becoming impractical. My version features a tanto blade with a black titanium nitride finish, while other configurations of the Twist Tighe have double-edged blades and more colorful scale options.

Size and weight are also massive differences from other automatics. At just 1.6 ounces with a 2.65-inch blade and about a 4-inch closed length, it’s remarkably small for an OTF knife and easy to carry daily. However, people with large hands may find it a bit compact.

Overall, the Twist Tighe combines premium materials like CPM MagnaCut steel with one of the smoothest actions I’ve experienced. If you’re looking for a compact, high-quality OTF automatic for everyday carry, it’s an excellent choice.

Recent findings suggest that the CRKT Minimalist Nessmuk combines the classic look of an outdoor blade with everyday convenience—plus there are several carry options for its sheath. It’s also surprisingly affordable for the build quality, priced at well under $100, with 12C27 stainless steel that keeps the cost down while providing corrosion resistance and easy sharpening.

In a recent development, another thing in its favor is its versatility beyond hunting season. Thanks to its broad belly, it excels at slicing food, carving wood, breaking down cardboard, and cutting cordage.

With three deep finger choils in the G10 handle, it remained comfortable in hand while I tested it, and the textured scales provided better grip than many larger knives with smoother handles. That may not be the case for folks with larger hands, however, considering the size of the handle. Still, for most people, it’s an excellent choice for a fixed blade that can handle general tasks.

Testing and reviewing knives is a mostly subjective affair, despite all the ink spilled over steel hardness and the trade-offs between edge retention and durability. And with that in mind, I should highlight that these selections are made by one person and thus subject to my personal biases when it comes to pocket knives.

Recent findings suggest that while I’ve developed many idiosyncratic preferences over more than a decade of knife reviewing and 40 years plus of knife-using, the significant one is that I am a knife user before a knife enthusiast. I can appreciate a “cool” knife design as much as any other knife nut that owns hundreds of knives, but I’m partial to folding designs that work well, fit my hand, and make my life easier in their role as an essential daily use tool.

Recent findings suggest that we update this guide multiple times throughout the year, and I’m constantly testing newly introduced pocket knives to look for new models that are worthy enough to unseat the favorites—and I don’t do that lightly. Year-round testing allows for longer-term use instead of a couple days of fidgeting with a blade and writing up a review. Most of the pocket knives featured here have been in my pocket on and off for months if not years, tackling everyday tasks as well as seasonal jobs such as butchering an elk or deer (if I’m lucky). We’ve included knives from the downright cheap to prohibitively expensive, but all the knives featured are ones we feel deliver good value considering the price tier.

As a baseline for any latest knife, I check the factory edge for sharpness, look for corrosion resistance with a saltwater bath and air drying, and (when feasible) disassemble the knife to better understand the lock and open/close mechanisms. After beating up a knife for a while, I also sharpen the blade with stones with an angle guide to find out just how easy it is to return the blade to sharp. One of my favorite tests is handing a knife to friends and strangers to see how regular people react to opening and closing one for the first time, since I spend more time with knives than most.

Recent findings suggest that choosing blade steel is where knife geeks can get into the weeds. There are trade-offs, though, with any type of steel. Broadly speaking, if you go with a softer steel it means the blade may get dull more easily but it's also easier to sharpen. Harder types of steel hold an edge longer but might be trickier for novices to sharpen at home.

Steel characteristics also affect how prone a blade will be to rusting; however, most decent modern pocket knives use a steel that’s rust-resistant enough that it won't require lots of special care. Almost all knives’ product pages will list the type of steel used, and if they don’t, it’s likely a budget knife. If you can’t find the steel online, check knife marketplace sites such as BladeHQ for the make and model.

Here are the highlights for some of the more common pocket knife steel types:.

Recent findings suggest that handle material is also an important choice. Wood is less common these days and less durable than steel or lighter, more durable synthetic materials like G10 and carbon fiber. Still, you may prefer the feel and look of wood despite the drawbacks. Steel is strong and durable but adds weight which can be a positive or a negative depending on how you use the knife and what you prefer hanging on your pocket.

Industry observers note that A knife’s dimensions and weight affect the fit in your hand and ease of use. In general, bigger hands won’t like tiny knives and vice versa, but how and where you carry a knife impact your preferences for size and weight. If you’re an office executive, you may not want an oversized, obvious blade for daily carry, while working on a farm or in the trades, you might prefer a bigger, burlier blade to stand up to prying tasks and day-to-day abuse.

It has been revealed that the action of a pocket knife can play an outsized role in your appreciation for it. I routinely test a lot of folding knives and find the knives I reach for most often are ones that are the most (subjectively) satisfying—and that I can easily operate one-handed when my off hand is busy doing something else. If you carry it long enough, you’ll get proficient with most any knife, but each of these common mechanisms has its strengths and weaknesses to consider.

In the previous century, secure locking mechanisms weren’t common, but today they’re expected if not universal. Classic knives, such as Case’s beloved Stockman and Victorinox’s iconic Swiss Army Knife, use slip joints, which hold the blade open but don’t truly lock. Because of the increased safety of a locking blade, I recommend choosing a pocket knife with some kind of a locking mechanism. If you are comfortable with a slip joint or other non-locking blade and enjoy the style, by all means, buy one. Note that your choice of lock typically dictates how you close the knife, so this will have a major impact on how easy it is to operate.

In a recent development, if cost is a major factor for you, it will quickly narrow the range of options. Knives can range in cost from just a few dollars to hundreds or even thousands for custom and limited edition options from celebrated knifemakers. Most people, however, will be looking at what are called “production knives”—models that are mass-produced, usually in a factory instead of by hand from individual knifemakers. While these blades can still run up to $500 or so, the range is much tighter as the cost to produce is lower.

Sources indicate that knives for less than about $20 will usually feature softer, cheaper steels and inexpensive handles. These knives may have less quality control than pricier models, but you can still get a decent knife from an established manufacturer any day of the week for less than $50. For example, the cheapest knife I recommend costs about $25.

Choosing a pocket knife with harder carbon steel will usually push the price closer to $100 or more. Go past that $100 price point, and you’re paying for specific designs, brand names, and other personal preferences, but you’ll start to see diminishing returns as far as raw functionality.

According to recent reports, in the United States, carrying most pocket knives won’t break any laws. But each state has its own rules that might restrict the specific pocket knives you can legally carry. Many states have prohibitions on certain automatic knives, on blade length, and even on whether or not you can carry certain knives concealed.

Recent findings suggest that the American Knife and Tool Institute has a helpful state-by-state guide to knife laws you can consult. Traveling abroad brings an even wider range of regulations, as some countries such as Austria have almost no restrictions while Norway (despite a rich knifemaking heritage) has an outright ban on carrying knives in urban areas.

In a recent development, possibly. First, not all pocket knives are the same. The legal definition of pocket knives may vary across states and at the federal level which can impact shipment and receipt.

Industry observers note that most states also have some kind of restrictions on what knives you can carry on your person. Even in wild west Colorado where I live, it is illegal to carry a blade longer than 3.5 inches “concealed” which would include “in your pocket.” In Upcoming York state where I grew up, switchblades are illegal and you must be a U.S. citizen to even own a knife, but there are no concealed carry restrictions. Check your state laws here.

Outside of local laws, consider how a knife fits in your hand. A knife that feels tiny and awkward to someone with large hands might be perfect for someone else. If you’re not already a regular pocket knife carrier, stop into an outdoors store where you can handle a wide range of knives and see what feels good. Most people will feel comfortable with blades in the 2.5- to 3-inch range, though folks with larger hands may want something bigger.

I’ll start with a caution—that you may not want a surgically sharp pocket knife. Because I use my pocket knife so frequently and casually, I don’t like to be as cautious as you have to be with an ultra-sharp blade.

I experimented with carrying a replaceable blade knife for a few months and I ended up giving myself several minor but annoying slices. That mentioned, any knife will eventually require sharpening. Most pocket knives have a fairly obtuse 20-degree or higher blade angle, which makes them less challenging to sharpen yourself.

Sources indicate that knife sharpening is a skill that’s not easy to master (learn how here), but there are tools available to help. While whetstone sharpening is soothing in a Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance sort of way, you probably already have a pull-through sharpener somewhere (check kitchen drawers).

These sharpeners aren’t the perfect sharpening solution, but they’re relatively idiot-proof and good enough to perk up your blade. If all of this sounds like something you’ll never bother with, there are lots of mail-in sharpening services such as The Sharp Brothers, who will professionally sharpen your blades for a fee. Also, many manufacturers offer similar services. Benchmade, for example, has a LifeSharp program that gives you free sharpening for any Benchmade knife. Some manufacturers such as Kershaw also offer blade replacement (often for a fee) if you’ve broken or otherwise damaged your blade beyond repair.

It has been revealed that this is both a surprisingly common and difficult-to-answer question. Obviously personal budget comes into play, but so do your preferences. Despite considering myself a pocket knife enthusiast, I carried a cheap pocket knife from Walmart for years that cost me literally $1. The organization raised the price to $2 at some point. Those knives would rust at the hinge, but they did the trick and were great for putting in my checked luggage. I wouldn’t worry about losing it at my destination and wouldn’t cry if the TSA took it.

According to recent reports, while I can’t recommend buying $2 knives in good conscience for most circumstances, quality options such as the Coast Contra recommended above can be had for under $20. If you’re new to knives, start out with something cheaper, definitely under $50, until you develop strong opinions about the pocket knife you prefer.

  • Industry observers note that yian Yin seeks to understand the dynamics of science itself.
  • “I want to understand what the secret sources or recipes of success are,” says Yin, of Cornell University.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Industry observers note that yian Yin seeks to understand the dynamics of science itself. The computational social scientist is particularly interested in how innovations happen and how they may be accelerated.

“I want to understand what the secret sources or recipes of success are,” says Yin, of Cornell University.

Recent findings suggest that he applied machine learning techniques to accepted and rejected research proposals to understand how scientists learn from failures. What he found was that scientists fail, and they fail often. Some switched gears after some rejections, but others who continued their research and incorporated feedback found success at a faster rate. Those who changed ideas or scrapped original proposals did not leverage a lot from their experience.

“A group that’s not only failing better and better,” Yin claims, “is also failing faster and increasingly faster towards their eventual success.”.

Industry observers note that more recently, Yin has been investigating how generative AI is changing scientific publishing. Journals are receiving more AI-assisted submissions than ever before, which is leading the peer-review process to falter. More seemingly well-written papers that lack substance are getting through, he found. Coming up with large-scale solutions requires looking at the glitch in a measurable way, Yin says.

“Considering both the technological and social side of scientific ecosystems would be something that’s really beneficial for the ongoing public debate and discussion about how we accelerate science in the age of artificial intelligence,” Yin says.

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1408 w)

Some of the most effective treatments for back pain are also the most affordable

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1408 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A review involving nearly 15,000 people suggests that several drug-free treatments for lower back pain can improve health outcomes and reduce overall costs.
  • Treatments such as yoga, acupuncture, and cognitive therapy might seem like added expenses for people with lower back pain.
  • However, a upcoming review suggests that these approaches can improve health outcomes while reducing overall costs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A review involving nearly 15,000 people suggests that several drug-free treatments for lower back pain can improve health outcomes and reduce overall costs.

Treatments such as yoga, acupuncture, and cognitive therapy might seem like added expenses for people with lower back pain.

However, a upcoming review suggests that these approaches can improve health outcomes while reducing overall costs.

Researchers reached that conclusion after reviewing 20 papers covering 24 studies and 14,884 people.

Eight treatments that use no drugs and no surgery were both more effective and less costly than usual care in at least one way of counting the costs.

The authors wrote that these treatments are still far from routine in most countries.

Manuela Ferreira, a professor at the George Institute for Global Health in Sydney, was the senior author. Her team included researchers at the University of Sydney and the University of Warwick in England.

“Low back pain is the world’s leading cause of disability, but many effective treatments can also save healthcare dollars,” Ferreira remarked.

“Our review found that approaches such as exercise, yoga, acupuncture and psychological support can help people recover while providing good value for money.”.

According to recent reports, pain in the lower back is the leading cause of disability worldwide, and treating it costs a lot. In Australia, back problems accounted for about 2.2% of all health spending in the 2020 to 2021 financial year.

The team searched ten research databases for studies that compared what a treatment cost with what it achieved. They kept only treatments backed by at least one of three major guidelines.

Those come from the World Health Organization, the United Kingdom’s National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, known as NICE, and the North American Spine Society.

It has been revealed that benefit was measured in a unit that combines how long a person lives with how well they live during that time. Health economists call it a quality-adjusted life year.

Recent findings suggest that the team converted every cost to 2024 British pounds and used the same cutoff NICE uses. A treatment counted as worth paying for if each extra year of healthy life cost less than £20,000.

Twenty papers published between 2005 and 2026 met those criteria.

They covered 24 studies, 55 comparisons with usual care, and 14,884 people in nine high-income countries, most often the United Kingdom.

Usual care in these trials meant ordinary first-contact care: a doctor’s advice, a booklet, some medication, and sometimes a referral to a physical therapist.

Six single treatments came out both more effective and less costly than that.

They were yoga, acupuncture, cognitive therapy, support for people managing their own pain, education aimed at reducing fear of the pain, and mindfulness-based stress reduction.

Two combinations did the same: workplace advice paired with a gradual return to activity, and a program of diet and physical activity.

In an interview with Earth.com, Ferreira was asked what someone with back pain should ask a doctor first. She suggested two questions.

“Is there anything more serious causing my back pain? If not, which is the case for most people, can you teach me or refer me to someone who can teach me how to manage my own symptoms?” she stated.

In health economics, a treatment that is both more effective and less costly is described as dominant.

In the whole review, only one comparison went the other way, and that was a British massage program.

Massage cost about £324 more per person than usual care in 2024 money, and it gained no extra healthy time at all.

Whether a treatment saves money depends on whose bills get counted.

The review sorted every result three ways: the health system’s costs, an insurer’s or employer’s costs, and society’s costs, which add in lost wages and missed work.

In a recent development, A British yoga trial reveals why that matters. In it, 313 people with chronic or recurring back pain were offered 12 weekly group classes.

Counting only health care, the classes added about £715 per person, and each extra year of healthy life cost about £19,300, just under the £20,000 bar.

Recent findings suggest that counting lost workdays too, the yoga group cost society about £293 less per person than the usual-care group. And the yoga group still gained more healthy time.

The biggest saving in the review came from a Dutch program for workers on sick leave with chronic back pain.

It paired workplace advice with a gradual return to activity, and it cut society’s costs by about £7,315 per person compared with usual care. An Australian cognitive therapy program cut them by about £2,671.

Savings like those count only when lost work is part of the sum.

A treatment did not have to save money to be considered cost-effective.

Counting the health system’s costs, 14 of 18 comparisons passed, including exercise alone, spinal manipulation, and exercise paired with cognitive therapy.

In a recent development, counting society’s costs, 15 of 19 passed, and counting an insurer’s or employer’s, 11 of 14 did. Passing was the rule, but confidence in each pass varied.

Where a study reported how likely its treatment was to be good value, the figure ran from 50% to 99.6%.

One of the clearest savings came from an enhanced course of acupuncture in the United States, with extra sessions added to a standard 12-week course. It cut health care costs by about £396 per person.

Acupuncture and massage were tested in many of the studies, and their results were inconsistent.

Recent findings suggest that the authors wrote that this points to context, who is paying, and how the treatment is delivered. A Belgian modeling study found osteopathy was dominant from a payer’s perspective.

Recent findings suggest that the three modeling studies in the review met far fewer items on their quality checklist than the trials met on theirs, though. The weakest of them met two of 57 items.

A review in 2011 of 26 studies reached a similar verdict on some of these treatments, including exercise, acupuncture, and cognitive behavioral therapy.

Nine new economic evaluations have come out since the most recent review of the topic, in 2019.

The authors wrote that theirs is the first to cover every treatment the current guidelines recommend, measured against usual care.

Ferreira’s team wrote that yoga, acupuncture, cognitive behavioral therapy, and treatments aimed at reducing fear and stress still aren’t routinely offered or paid for in most countries.

Working out why, the team wrote, should be the next focus.

Asked what surprised her most, Ferreira mentioned it was that these treatments are not always available to patients.

“I was pleased to see so many options can benefit both patients and society,” Ferreira noted.

“The good news for people with back pain is that some of the most effective treatments are also among the most cost-effective.”.

“Investing in evidence-based care such as exercise, physical therapies and psychological support could help more people get better while reducing pressure on health systems.”.

Every one of the 24 studies came from a high-income country, so the authors wrote that their findings are unlikely to carry over to lower-income settings.

Ferreira noted testing them in poorer countries would take fresh trials and studies with local patients, clinicians, and policymakers.

Those would check that the treatments are safe, suited to local conditions, and acceptable.

Costs are tied to the health system that recorded them, and the studies measured them too differently to pool into one estimate.

Some people were left out by design. Studies of sciatica, where the pain runs down the leg, weren’t included, and neither were people who had back surgery in the past year.

Out-of-pocket costs, community services, and lost work were reported less often than the treatment’s price.

The larger gap is in what the review had nothing to compare. Not one of the studies that met its criteria tested a drug, an injection, or an operation for chronic pain in the back. Those treatments are paid for all over the world.

“We have not found studies on guideline endorsed pharmacological or surgical interventions for low back pain and therefore highlight the urgent need for those as well,” Ferreira told Earth.com.

The authors wrote that future studies should count lost work and community costs too.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Medicine.

Breaking: What’s Your Airport Dwell Time? A Metric Businesses Think A Lot About

📅 01 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (944 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Godsavethepoints

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that dwell time, simply, is how long you spend in an airport, or airport space, before a flight.
  • Industry observers note that for businesses in air travel and airports, like lounge operators, credit card companies or airlines, it’s one of the main things they think about.
  • More importantly, the tracking of that dwell time has contributed to quite a lot of innovation in lounges and airports, with hopefully much more to come.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that dwell time, simply, is how long you spend in an airport, or airport space, before a flight. For most people, it’s not something they’ve ever actively really thought about.

Industry observers note that for businesses in air travel and airports, like lounge operators, credit card companies or airlines, it’s one of the main things they think about. So what’s yours and what does it say about you?

Well, a lot. More importantly, the tracking of that dwell time has contributed to quite a lot of innovation in lounges and airports, with hopefully much more to come.

In a recent development, build it and they will come. Who knew Kevin Costner knew so much about lounges?! In truth, if someone builds a lounge, everyone will come and ensuring it’s a good experience is an art form requiring math. Crowds can be hard to predict and most lounges are “too” full these days.

Knowing the average dwell time of a customer, and even a specific customer profile is one of the best tools lounges have to predict the flows of customers, including how much they’ll need to stock in food and drinks and everything else during peak times.

Even outside of lounges, knowing how long an air traveler spends in the airport is vital to understanding what kind of businesses, restaurants or concessions to offer. There’s a reason grab and go places do really, really well and get away with charging $12 for water.

Surprisingly to some, top tier frequent flyers typically have a really low dwell time compared to lower ranks or leisure travelers.

Recent findings suggest that if an airline knows their lounge is full of top tiers that day, they can expect many people who won’t stay long. Whereas, if it’s a day with full flights and mostly leisure travel passengers, you can predict people will dwell far longer.

It makes sense. If you’re not used to the delights of a great airport lounge you come earlier, stay longer and take advantage of more. You also have less confidence in timings of the check in and security process, so you pad time in, in addition to the natural, “treat yourself” vibes.

If you do it all the time, every minute not in the airport is often seen as the win, so lounges are just a place to swiftly reset and refresh before carrying on.

Sources indicate that the first time I experienced a true first class lounge I think I got to the airport at the earliest possible interval. I had hours in there and of course, tried everything.

Recent findings suggest that but I’ve been very lucky, I’ve experienced most lounges many times, been spoiled by the best many times, and unless there’s a real wow factor moment, I’m happiest spending as little time waiting in an airport as possible. Don’t get me wrong, I still indulge from time to time, but I’ve seen a huge dip in my own dwell average.

Recent findings suggest that as I strolled through T2 at Heathrow this week en route to the United Club, it occurred to me that most of my recent lounge visits averaged about 30 minutes in total. In that 30 minutes I’d say I have a maximum of one drink, often little or no food, and mostly take advantage of the wifi and nice calm facilities.

I’ve gotten my time from curb to security at Heathrow down to a decent science and I like it that way. At other airports with even more predictable security and check in patterns, I’ll shave even more time off, often leaving no time for lounges at all.

Sources indicate that and this raises a fair question: if everyone could truly model out their time from curb to airside, would they spend as long? Things like TSA PreCheck and CLEAR have been monumental in adding a layer of certainty to this process and I’d expect we’ll see more of it. Will more passengers change habits as they have better confidence in making their flight while cutting it fine?

Now of course, all bets are off when I travel with my kids. And that’s kind of the point. We think we’re very unique in our travel habits, but there are many variables of our travels which drop us into a fairly predictable pattern … and dwell time.

When lounge access is a marquee benefit of being a frequent flyer, but most top frequent flyers hardly leave any time for lounge dwelling, is that a real selling point?

In response, we’ve seen really clever pivots lately, including from Air Canada and Capital One. Each brand has created curated “grab and go” offerings in their lounges or lounge-like areas to offer passengers complimentary things which have tangible value — a nitro cold brew latte, or a nice pastry — for “free”, which they’re totally able to take on the road with them.

Industry observers note that that’s a huge departure from the days of lounges with signs everywhere saying no outside food and drinks and no removing food or drinks from the lounge. People never paid attention anyway, and this now just creates a formalized and better thought out approach to catering to all traveler needs.

The massive question is: what’s next for adding value to a travelers airport journey? Be sure to share your lounge and travel habits as well.
