Industry News: One of Russia’s most active volcanoes rises above a sea of clouds

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A striking Landsat 9 image reveals the snow-covered summit and active lava dome of Shivelyuch volcano on Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula.
  • Today’s Image of the Day features one of Russia’s most active volcanoes rising above a blanket of clouds on the Kamchatka Peninsula.
  • Snow covers the upper slopes of Shivelyuch, while a dark formation near the summit offers a glimpse of the volcanic activity taking place within the mountain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A striking Landsat 9 image reveals the snow-covered summit and active lava dome of Shivelyuch volcano on Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula.

Today’s Image of the Day features one of Russia’s most active volcanoes rising above a blanket of clouds on the Kamchatka Peninsula.

Snow covers the upper slopes of Shivelyuch, while a dark formation near the summit offers a glimpse of the volcanic activity taking place within the mountain.

The image was captured on November 8, 2026, by the Operational Land Imager aboard Landsat 9. Although clouds concealed much of the surrounding landscape, the volcano’s summit remained visible from space.

The contrast between the snowy mountainside and the exposed volcanic rock offers a striking portrait of a landscape that is continually being rebuilt from within.

Shivelyuch, also known as Shiveluch, is among the largest and most active volcanoes on the Kamchatka Peninsula in Russia’s Far East.

The mountain has a complex geological history. Its older structure, known as Stary Shiveluch, dates back roughly 65,000 years.

A younger volcanic complex, Molodoy Shiveluch, subsequently developed within the remains of the older mountain.

The Smithsonian Institution’s Global Volcanism Program has documented at least 60 major eruptions at Shivelyuch during the Holocene, the geological epoch that began approximately 11,700 years ago.

Successive eruptions and collapses have left extensive deposits of volcanic material across the surrounding terrain. These deposits preserve a record of the mountain’s turbulent past.

One of the most intriguing features of Shivelyuch is its enormous caldera, a depression measuring approximately 5.6 miles (nine kilometers) across.

It has been revealed that within this depression, a lava dome has developed as magma reaches the surface. The dome stands out against the snow in the satellite image.

Unlike the fluid lava commonly associated with Hawaiian volcanoes, the thick lava that builds volcanic domes does not travel easily across the landscape.

Instead, it accumulates around the opening from which it emerges.

As more material reaches the surface, the dome can expand, develop fractures, and become increasingly unstable.

Sections of these domes sometimes collapse. Such events can unleash pyroclastic flows – rapidly moving mixtures of scorching gas, ash, and fragmented rock that sweep down a volcano’s slopes.

The process can dramatically alter the appearance of a mountain, sometimes within minutes.

Kamchatka’s extraordinary volcanic landscape owes its existence to the movement of enormous sections of Earth’s outer shell.

The peninsula sits along the Pacific Ring of Fire, a vast region of geological activity surrounding much of the Pacific Ocean.

Here, the Pacific tectonic plate descends beneath another plate in a process called subduction.

Water released from the descending plate promotes melting in the overlying mantle, generating magma that can eventually rise toward the surface.

Over millions of years, this process has created a remarkable concentration of volcanoes, along with hot springs, geysers, and other geothermal features.

Kamchatka provides scientists with an opportunity to observe some of the fundamental processes responsible for reshaping Earth’s surface.

The effects of volcanic activity at Shivelyuch can extend well beyond the peninsula.

Although volcanic ash resembles ordinary dust, it consists of tiny fragments of rock, minerals, and volcanic glass.

These abrasive particles can damage aircraft engines and other critical equipment.

In a recent development, high-altitude winds can carry ash clouds across international borders and oceans. In July 2026, ash from Shivelyuch reached Alaskan airspace after traveling across the Bering Sea, disrupting air travel.

Even between major explosions, previously deposited ash can become airborne again when strong winds sweep across the landscape.

This means that an ash plume does not necessarily indicate that a newly introduced explosive eruption has occurred.

Volcanic activity at Shivelyuch had persisted for several months when Landsat 9 acquired this image.

Monitoring a remote volcano surrounded by unpredictable weather presents considerable challenges.

Satellites offer scientists an invaluable perspective on places where direct observations are difficult.

In addition to capturing changes in the appearance of volcanic landscapes, instruments aboard some satellites can detect infrared radiation associated with unusually hot surfaces.

These measurements help researchers identify areas of elevated temperature that may be associated with freshly exposed lava or other volcanic activity.

By comparing observations collected over extended periods, scientists can also track the growth and destruction of lava domes, map volcanic deposits, and document changes to the surrounding environment.

Weather clouds can interfere with many of these observations, making clear views of active volcanic features particularly valuable.

In a recent development, seen from hundreds of miles above Earth, Shivelyuch appears almost serene. Its snow-covered slopes emerge from the clouds, revealing a rugged summit seemingly isolated from the world below.

Yet the mountain’s appearance belies the geological activity taking place beneath its surface.

The dark lava dome visible in today’s image represents the latest chapter in a history of destruction and renewal spanning thousands of years.

Long after the surrounding clouds have dispersed, the forces responsible for building Shivelyuch will continue to transform the mountain.

Image Credit: NASA Earth Observatory /Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that fall is peak season for those who want to gather last-minute information on deer and other game animals ahead of hunting seasons. Even if you’re not heading into the woods to hunt, it’s one of the most interesting times of year for observing wild animals. Whitetail deer, elk, bears, and other animals are becoming much more active due to seasonal mating periods while waterfowl and other birds migrate for the winter.

The advantage of having a modern trail camera is the ability to capture the action you’d otherwise miss, whether it’s an elusive buck passing by your stand in the night or the raccoon creating backyard mayhem. If you’re considering a trail camera that uses a cellular network to send photos and videos directly to your smartphone, the good news is these have gotten even easier to use.

According to recent reports, while the trail cam experience improves every year, the cost of many units is more than $100, and cellular models require recurring data strategy charges, making it trickier to assess value. Images from game cameras are better than ever, even in budget models, and apps add software features often.

Sorting out what matters most to you and how you initiative to use your trail cameras can be a challenge, so we explain what to look for along with sharing our top recommendations selected from year-round testing of dozens of cameras evaluated side-by-side.

According to recent reports, the Tactacam Reveal Pro 4.0 replaces the Reveal Pro 3.0 camera, our previous pick for Best Overall. Released this summer, the Pro 4.0 version keeps what made the 3.0 great and improves on it in two key areas: image quality and battery life. Reveal has one of the best apps in the space, with tons of settings and features to tweak your setup and manage your cameras and images. Updates to these basics are big usability improvements that demanding trail camera consumers will notice.

Sources indicate that cameras going dead in the field is a major gripe for people of these gadgets. You have to physically go and replace batteries, which adds hassle and cost to your experience. I tend to place cameras in early summer and let them run for several months until my hunting season starts. The problem is that active cameras can run through eight to 12 AA batteries in a month depending on the model and your camera settings.

Tactacam has tackled this concern in a few ways with the Pro 4.0 release. The brand told me it audited everything about camera operation that drained the battery and then made small tweaks to reduce power demands anywhere it could.

Tactacam has also developed sold separately R5 and R10 lithium battery packs that replace previous battery add-ons, which have the notable benefit of swapping into the same form factor as the AA battery tray, so they don’t add bulk to the camera.

In a recent development, image quality in the Reveal cameras has always been solid, but the firm took a unique approach to dealing with the challenge of getting both crisp day and night images by installing separate sensors for each. Photographers know that night images require different gear and settings than daylight shooting, so the split makes sense. The early returns from a month of testing confirm that the quality of both day and night is much improved.

According to recent reports, the rest of this flagship Reveal camera is impressive, carrying over from the Pro 3.0 and now-discontinued Ultra camera. The Reveal lineup now has just two similar cameras: the Pro 4.0 and the X 4.0. The Reveal X 4.0 is basically the Pro 4.0 without a built-in display screen, which saves $30 and is a great option if you don’t value the screen for aiming and reviewing images at the device.

As mentioned, the robust app gives you remote control over everything including photo and video capture settings, transmission frequency, night image flash, trigger delays, and more. You’re also able to launch a live stream to follow up on interesting images, but there’s an additional subscription cost and it will drain the battery quickly. There’s also built-in GPS that indicates the location of your camera on a map within the app—essential if you’ve forgotten where you placed it or if it’s stolen.

Full Tactacam Reveal Pro 4.0 Review.

Cell-connected trail cameras are handy, but if you’re low on funds or trying to run a multitude of cameras, paying $150 and up per camera gets pricey fast. Spypoint’s Flex M2 trail camera keeps both the upfront purchase cost and recurring subscription fees reasonable. Spypoint even has a free data strategy that gives you 100 images per month if you want to avoid subscription fees altogether. (The Flex M2 doesn’t have onboard memory, nor does it ship with an SD card, so you’ll have to spend at least another $20 per camera for a high-speed SD card.).

Sources indicate that despite the low price, the camera’s 32-megapixel photos and 1080p video are clear and well-exposed. The Flex M2 displays lower-resolution images in the app but you can request full-resolution images when you want more detail. This is beneficial because it keeps data demands low and highlights up in the battery usage as well. After a month in the field, the eight AA batteries I was using displayed in the app at “High” strength.

Additionally, I appreciated that this camera is compact since I’m usually hauling my cameras several miles into the backcountry in a pack. If you want to run this camera year-round, I’d consider picking up the $60 five-watt solar panel add-on, which has a built-in battery and should allow you to leave the Flex M2 up indefinitely.

I was impressed with the overall experience with the Flex M2, but the highlight here is the cost to purchase and run this camera. Yes, you’ll need to pay up for video or a higher quota of images, but this is a great option if you want the excitement of getting trail camera images on your phone without the annoyance of yet another recurring subscription fee on your credit card.

There are two significant recurring costs with a cellular trail camera: the data initiative and batteries. Connected cameras can chew through batteries, which can add up, especially since you’ll want to use more expensive lithium batteries if you can. Sehmua’s 4G Solar Trail Camera comes with rechargeable batteries and a solar panel, which allows the camera to run indefinitely given adequate sun exposure.

The camera itself has a fast trigger and 2K photo and video that can be saved to an SD card, or to cloud storage for an additional cost. The app, which is a little clunky and can be confusing due to some quirky menus and word choices, works with images that show up rapidly and reliably.

Notably, even though this is a 4G cellular-connected camera, you can still use the camera to record to the SD card if you decide not to pay for one of the data prepares. This is another sneaky way this camera provides solid value for its low price point.

Full Sehmua Trail Camera Review.

Industry observers note that the best way to cut down on battery costs for your trail cameras is running solar panels. While many cameras have the option to run on solar, it’s often an additional upfront cost. The new 2026 Moultrie Edge 4 Solar trail camera has it all smartly packaged together in an integrated unit that costs less than some standalone cameras.

Recent findings suggest that setting up solar often requires separate mounting as well as hauling out lots of separate pieces and cables to be connected. The Edge 4 Solar just straps to a tree as a single unit, ready to run indefinitely. The camera comes with a rechargeable lithium-ion battery powered by the panel, which enables you to place a camera and leave it running as long as you need. Having the solar panel integrated is convenient and compact, but you’ll need to choose spots wisely to ensure both good captures and sun exposure.

Industry observers note that beyond the solar power setup, the Edge 4 is a solid trail camera with crisp 40-megapixel photos and 1080p video. The app is polished and makes setup and use hassle-free even if you’re not particularly tech-savvy. The subscription plans are in line with the industry average, ranging from $8.99 to $22.99. The lowest-tier plan offers more than most other companies’ $5 plans (1,000 images and 10 videos) and the most expensive plan offers unlimited images and 50 videos and discounts steeply to $7.99 per month for each additional camera.

The convenience of cell-connected trail cameras is undeniable, but if you’re burned out on subscription charges and don’t mind checking your cameras manually, you can save a significant amount on your trail camera setup. The WOSPORTS Trail Camera is a budget option with impressive image quality and low one-time cost. The camera doesn’t ship with the required eight AA batteries, but it does come with an SD card.

This compact G600 records imagery to an SD card and lasts longer since it doesn’t use batteries communicating over cellular networks. You’ll have to walk into your hunting zone to swap cards, but the purchase price is a fraction of the lifetime cost of buying and operating a modern cell-connected setup.

Recent findings suggest that the 56-megapixel images and 4K video aren’t Planet Earth–level quality, but I was still more than satisfied with the pictures and videos I got. I don’t put too much stock in megapixel numbers as a true measure of trail camera image quality because these numbers are mostly inflated with software enhancements. That said, the images and videos from the WOSPORTS camera were sharp enough for clear identification of details.

The Defend by Reveal 360 is not your traditional trail camera—it’s closer to a home security camera that’s designed to work anywhere. Ring and other doorbell cameras usually rely on WiFi for connectivity, which makes them impractical more than about 50 yards from your router. The Defend 360 uses cellular networks instead so you can place this camera anywhere with a decent cell signal.

According to recent reports, in the field, the Defend 360’s biggest advantage is motion. Most trail cams are fixed in place, but this one adds remote pan-and-tilt control, allowing you to reposition the camera from your phone. Its 355-degree pan and 75-degree tilt effectively eliminate blind spots when combined with the wide-angle lens.

Like a regular trail camera, motion detection triggers photos only to conserve battery and data. A 1080p live view can be activated on demand when you need a closer live look. That approach makes sense for remote monitoring, though it feels different if you’re used to continuous video feeds from home security cameras.

Recent findings suggest that A rechargeable battery and included solar panel allow for long-term deployment with minimal maintenance. Setup is straightforward via the app, and the camera automatically connects to the strongest available carrier via eSIM.

Sources indicate that there are a few downsides. Night footage is serviceable but not amazing, and like most cellular cameras, it requires a subscription plan to unlock full functionality. Still, if your goal is reliable, wide-area monitoring in remote locations, the Defend 360 delivers better coverage and control than standard trail cameras.

A lifetime warranty usually isn’t reason enough alone to buy a product, but in the world of electronics generally and with trail cameras specifically, it’s unheard of and fairly compelling.

With Yellowstone.ai’s Y2 Camera and Solar Bundle, your upfront cost is on the higher side at $250, but the solar panel and rechargeable battery mean no recurring battery costs. You’ll also save on gas and time, since this is a cell-connected camera, and there’s no need to visit the camera unless you want to move it.

Compared to the significant-name trail camera apps, the app is not quite as polished, but over several months of testing, I did not experience any of the quirks and bugs I’ve experienced with some trail cam apps from overseas companies (Yellowstone.ai is U.S.-based).

According to recent reports, the image and video quality isn’t quite as sharp as the top tier of the cameras I’ve tested like the Reveal Pro 4.0 or Moultrie Edge 4 Solar, but it’s by no means unacceptable. I was impressed by features such as built-in GPS, automatic cell network selection, and remote settings adjustments.

The solar bundle comes with the panel, Y2 camera, and two rechargeable battery packs. If you want to keep the upfront cost down, the camera alone is half the price at $125.

It has been revealed that no matter how great your trail camera placement, it’s easy for cameras to miss animals. This is exacerbated in significant open areas such as wetlands or crop fields where it can be hard to know precisely where animals might appear.

Muddy’s Trifecta 180 is built to minimize these misses. Three motion sensors and a rotating camera capture wide-angle 180-degree images. This is the perfect camera for the edge of large agricultural fields where animals could appear anywhere and often turn up in groups that can be hard to capture in a single image. You have the option for the camera to stitch together impressive panorama images (though they’re harder to appreciate on a phone screen) or the option to capture single-zone images like a regular trail camera would.

The downside of this impressive device is that it seemed to use more battery power than usual, likely attributable to the camera’s need to move and the usual drains of taking and transmitting images. If you’re planning on running it long-term, I’d consider picking up the solar panel accessory with integrated battery.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve assembled my choices in this guide based on years of firsthand testing, and I continue testing fresh trail cam options every season to keep up with the constant rollout of new features and improvements. For decades, I’ve been hanging trail cameras with professional hunters and friends to capture wallowing elk, nursing moose, and scavenging bears on camera.

Historically, I’ve preferred inexpensive, simple cameras that I monitor manually, which keeps my trail camera budget in check, but as connected cameras have gotten more reliable and affordable, I’ve shifted to using cell cams almost exclusively. I hunt in three different states as well as in spots several hours from my home in Colorado, which makes manually checking all my cameras nearly impossible. I still employ “manual” cameras around my property where pulling memory cards frequently isn’t a pain.

Recent findings suggest that one of the main divisions in the trail camera market is whether your trail camera connects to a cellular network, which, if it does, is what allows you to wirelessly send images over great distances. Connected models are so common now that AT&T and Verizon offer monthly service intends that often come bundled with the camera.

It has been revealed that this connectivity means that you don’t have to physically visit your camera to check out the imagery it has captured—a benefit that’s most tangible when cameras are placed in far-flung hunting spots, but less valuable if you’re using the camera closer to your house. The cellular connection also makes the cameras easier to operate since most cell-connected cameras can be controlled via your smartphone through apps. These allow you to use remote-control camera settings to switch between photo and video modes, adjust camera sensitivity, and check battery levels.

Sources indicate that networked cameras are addictive to use because they can provide instant, or at least frequent, gratification from your camera(s). However, there’s usually a recurring data plan cost in addition to setup complexity. Bottom line: Be sure you really need the connectivity. There also may be legal restrictions on wirelessly connected cameras that limit how you can use them. Be sure to double-check your state’s regulations before buying.

In a recent development, all trail cameras store images locally on the device, whether or not they have the ability to transmit them wirelessly. More often than not, that storage comes in the form of an SD or micro SD card, which you can remove to download your photos. Cameras with wireless support, however, now often feature an internal hard drive, which stores data more reliably, since you no longer need to physically “pull cards” to collect your footage.

If you’re planning to only use a networked camera, I recommend choosing a camera with internal memory. The No. 1 source of problems I’ve had over the years of testing dozens of different trail cameras and helping others set up many more is memory cards. These plastic chip-like cards are fragile, easy to lose, and can be formatted incorrectly. Even when there’s nothing wrong with a card, cheaper SD cards with slower transfer speeds can cause errors when processing larger images and videos.

According to recent reports, the only advantage of having a camera with removable memory is if you want to use the camera without a data blueprint. This is required for the increasingly rare non-networked cameras, but even connected cameras can be used manually if they have physical cards. Some cameras with internal memory also have an optional SD card slot, such as the Reveal Pro 3.0, which gives you the option to expand storage capacity and use the camera without paying for a data plan.

Sources indicate that this might seem like a minor detail, but given that many people want their trail camera to capture their subjects without alerting those subjects to the camera’s presence, the camera’s exterior color can be a critical factor. Since a majority of trail cameras are marketed to hunters and are intended to be used outdoors, these devices generally come in solid earth tones or camouflage patterns.

If you’re a hunter, you probably already have a good sense of what patterns are most appropriate for your area. If not, snap some photos of the trunks of the trees where you intend to mount the camera; then compare them to the patterns on the cameras you’re considering.

Sources indicate that cameron Shrum, avid bowhunter and co-owner of C&K Archery in Frisco, Colorado, says, “People will get a good deal on a camera and not realize how notable it is to have [it] match [their] habitat. The goal is to get pictures of animals without them knowing they are being watched, and when something is out of place, game animals have a tendency to figure it out.”.

In a recent development, as a professional photographer and videographer, the first thing you need to know about judging the quality of a camera is that there is no single metric that easily tells you which camera will record more clearly. At a glance, checking specs like the number of megapixels in a camera’s sensor gives you a decent clue as to what you can expect.

It has been revealed that ultimately, the best way to gauge the quality of a trail camera is with your eyes. Take a minute to look at sample photos posted by customers on retailers such as Amazon, which give you a practical way to evaluate images taken under natural conditions.

Trail cameras rarely take print-worthy shots, but that isn’t what they’re for. If you’re just patterning animals, image quality isn’t as crucial as simply detecting them. Trophy hunters trying to identify certain calibers of animals or monitor a specific animal across multiple cameras will want to be more picky about image quality and clarity.

In a recent development, even if you don’t need great fidelity, a better image makes using trail cams more useful and rewarding. I’ve come to appreciate having modern trail cameras that deliver clear images and 4K videos over the crude, fuzzy work of older, lo-fi models.

I recommend using only lithium batteries in trail cameras. Especially with cheaper cameras, I’ve found that regular alkaline batteries don’t provide enough voltage for the IR flash, and many times a trail camera may not record video with underpowered batteries (alkaline batteries start decreasing in voltage as soon as you start using them). Lithium batteries deliver higher voltage consistently, and they work better in the cold.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re setting up a cellular trail cam, make sure you check signal strength in the area. If you have a camera that offers an app or website (as many now do) that lets you view images on your smartphone, try triggering the camera and see if you receive the notification and image.

Since trail cameras are often left alone for days, weeks, or even months at a time, setting them up properly is important. Shrum recommends testing your trail camera before you walk away. “Have it snap a few pictures with you walking by and then review them. Sometimes you may not have the right angle; it may be too high or too low. Try to set the height and angle to capture the game in the center of the camera’s view.”.

Trail cameras are usually strapped to a tree and most come packaged with a long strap for this purpose. If you’re placing a camera somewhere without convenient trees for the angle you want, look into a camera stand or even a tripod. Most trail cameras have a standard tripod plate mount (¼-20) and stands or stakes are available from most manufacturers.

A common spot to place cameras is along well-traveled game trails. A tip I picked up watching champion archer Levi Morgan put up cameras on one of his hunting leases: rather than pointing the camera down a trail where it’s likely to be in the line-of-sight of animals as they walk it, put the camera off-trail between 10 and 30 feet away perpendicular to the trail. This will usually give you broadside images of animals instead of head-on and puts the camera in their periphery.

Once you’ve tested your placement (and image transmission for connected cameras) by viewing a test photo on the app or the camera itself, scan the camera’s field of view for latest-growth vegetation. Plants and tree branches can result in a near-constant stream of false triggers on a windy day. I like to place any plants or branches I cut behind the camera for a bit of concealment, making sure they can’t blow in front of the camera.

It has been revealed that since trail cams are motion-activated, a fast trigger seems crucial. You don’t want an animal to pass by the camera before you get a photo, right? In my experience, the real problem is taking the photo too rapidly, which results in seeing just the nose of a slow-moving deer. Still, many brands tout their fast trigger speeds as if they solve an important problem.

“It’s kind of a BS spec, frankly,” Gregg Farrell, vice president of marketing for Tactacam Reveal, told me. “The goal is to capture the animal in the center of the frame and our cameras do that through the operating system working with the [motion] sensor.”.

Most trail cameras have listed trigger speeds around a half second, which can work well, but are often too quick if implemented poorly. I almost always switch my cameras to shoot a multishot burst, if available, to give the camera more opportunities to grab a well-framed shot. Keep in mind, though, that this will double or triple the number of images you receive, so it may not be a solution if you’re using a cell-connected camera and trying to save with a limited-data strategy.

Recent findings suggest that some cameras have detection delay settings that let you set a period of time after an image is captured before it’ll take another. This can cut down on look-alike images if an animal is hanging around in the detection area, especially if you’ve enabled a multishot mode.

Recent findings suggest that connected trail cameras make scouting convenient, but they come with hidden costs. Almost all cellular trail cameras require a monthly data initiative to cover the cost of cloud storage and image transmission.

Many companies tack on extra fees for features such as live streaming, which eat up a lot of data and cost the companies money with their network provider partners. Like sitting at a blackjack table, it’s easy to get caught up in the excitement of scouting and click your way to hundreds of dollars in recurring monthly charges. You can review the details of each company’s data plans before you buy and decide what features you want to use in advance. You can save money on a camera if you decide you don’t need all the latest features and avoid the temptation of activating those extra charges in the process.

Industry observers note that common game animals such as whitetail deer and elk tend to settle into routines during the summer months which often persist into early fall. The change of seasons and seasonal mating windows will help throw routine out the window in the fall, but if you can identify high-traffic areas in the spring and early summer, that will likely continue all summer.

In a recent development, the best practices for finding a good spot and setting up the camera properly are the same in any season. Spring in some ways makes it easier to identify animal travel patterns since the ground is often wet and recent activity is more obvious. Hike your zone and look for fresh signs to identify intersections, pinch points, and frequently visited locations. If you’re able to access your cameras easily and often, use the early season to experiment with different locations for a few weeks and try latest spots you hadn’t considered before that show promise based on animal signs. Half the fun of placing these cameras is finding that perfect location and image framing that yields a ton of exciting wildlife images.

There are plenty of things that can trigger a trail camera other than the type(s) of animals you’re looking to capture, including squirrels, lights, and vegetation moving in the wind. “False triggers,” as we call them, are not only disappointing, but waste storage and burn through your data plan. It’s hard to eliminate them completely, but there are lots of ways to minimize them.

Recent findings suggest that the most important is proper camera setup. Once you’ve got it framed up the way you want and have a successful test image, look for branches and weeds in the frame, primarily in the foreground. A single goldenrod stalk or pine bough can burn through a month’s data allotment on a windy day, so take your time to clear the immediate area in front of your camera.

Recent findings suggest that you can’t always clear cut in front of a camera, so if you find you’re still getting more false triggers than you’d like, adjust the camera’s trigger sensitivity down. Many cameras only offer high or low, but if you have a more finely graded adjustment such as the 1 through 10 sensitivity settings on the Reveal Pro 3.0, adjust slowly down until you stop getting false triggers so you don’t overcorrect and miss animals.

Some cameras also use recognition software to reject images that appear to be empty. Moultrie’s Edge cameras allow you to only accept motion triggers in selected zones of an image, effectively blocking triggers from, for example, a corner of a detection zone with moving tree branches.

Most states have some sort of regulation with the use of trail cameras, especially when used on public land and as they relate to hunting activities. Arizona, where game animals tend to congregate around limited water sources, banned trail cameras for hunting statewide in 2021. Colorado, where I live, has few restrictions on trail camera use before your hunting season begins, but limits employing them while you’re actively hunting.

Using trail cameras on your own private property doesn’t usually involve too many restrictions, but be sure to check the regulations from your state’s wildlife management organization to confirm, as private land practices can still be regulated through the hunting codes since wildlife are considered a shared public resource.

There are so many options for security cameras dedicated to home use, and because of that, most of the time it makes more sense to just buy a security camera from a brand that specializes in that application, such as Ring or Google Nest.

These products generally have superior apps and software to hunt-focused trail cameras. Since they're designed for home use, they effortlessly connect to your home WiFi network, don’t require a data subscription, and will have features trail cameras won’t such as two-way communication.

Recent findings suggest that that stated, if you already own trail cameras and don’t need specific features, most trail cameras can serve a security purpose. The best trail cameras to employ for security are the newer “live” trail cameras that transmit imagery instantly via cell networks and notify you on your phone when the camera has been triggered.

In a recent development, another option is WiFi-enabled trail cameras that can connect to your phone without a cellular network to transmit images. However, these cameras don’t usually transmit if you’re not within range of the camera (i.e., at home), so they’re limited to general monitoring rather than real-time notification when you’re away.

New Credit Card Sets Annual Fee Dynamically, Based On Benefit Usage

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes.
  • Since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep.
  • Signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes. “It feels like a coupon book” is often the consumer reaction, particularly as annual fees rise as justification for an increasing number of partner offer benefits, which if consumed in entirety could lead to more value.

Since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep. In a bold move, a newly introduced card launched today which offers a flexible annual fee, based only on the benefits you actually use.

Signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee? You’re not alone.

To quell this issue, the newly introduced card is effectively a build your own card, card.

It has been revealed that despite the innovation, the card draws on the historical concept of the coupon book, where you only pay for the offers you tear out and redeem. The annual fee starts at zero, but as you actually redeem the cards benefits, you get billed accordingly. Your fee can be zero, or as high as $10,000 per year.

Done right, you can end up paying $650 in annual fees for about $800 worth of stuff, some of which you wanted and most of which, about $700 worth, you didn’t really want or need, but felt compelled to get, just because it’s there.

This model allows you to really dive into the classic coupon book, feeling like you’re really tearing offers out of the page, and simply leaving the ones you’re not using in the book. You’re only paying for the ones you rip out, but when there’s so many offers to choose from, the book just feels so compelling.

Obviously, it’s April 1st and no such card is coming to the market (yet, lol), but hopefully this light hearted amusement has been a helpful exercise in framing the true value you’re really extracting from your premium credit card, or conversely, the lack thereof.

Consider the things you’d actually purchase without the “offer” prompt and if that number still adds up to be more than the annual fee, you’re doing it right. If it doesn’t….

#157464. Industry News: Surrounded by female cows, a bull named Achille chose to form a close bond with a male donkey named Patroclo that lasted for weeks, leaving scientists baffled

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1183 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Surrounded by female cows, a bull named Achille chose to form a close bond with a male donkey named Patroclo that lasted for weeks, leaving scientists baffled

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1183 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Achille the bull and Patroclo, a male donkey, mated and groomed each other for weeks in an Ethiopian pasture, forming a very unusual and mutual bond.
  • In a recent development, on a beautiful plateau in Ethiopia, a bull named Achille spent his days in a pasture full of female cows and other bulls.
  • This happened not once, not twice, but at least 51 times.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Achille the bull and Patroclo, a male donkey, mated and groomed each other for weeks in an Ethiopian pasture, forming a very unusual and mutual bond.

In a recent development, on a beautiful plateau in Ethiopia, a bull named Achille spent his days in a pasture full of female cows and other bulls. Yet over two weeks in March, researchers watched him ignore the females, and his own species, to mount a male donkey named Patroclo.

This happened not once, not twice, but at least 51 times.

Male cattle sometimes mount each other when no female cows are around, but Achille had plenty of them right beside him, and Patroclo never tried to get away.

The researchers concluded that the pair shared a selective, mutual bond, and that the mounting was part of it.

Elisabetta Palagi, an associate professor of biology at the University of Pisa in Italy, and her colleagues described the pair in a two-page report.

It has been revealed that martina Francesconi and André da Cruz, both PhD students at Pisa, are the lead authors. Da Cruz is also affiliated with CRIA, an anthropology research center in Lisbon.

Their report focuses on this one bull and one donkey, who they watched and studied very closely for eight days.

Sources indicate that in an interview with Earth.com, Palagi noted the team discovered the pair unexpectedly. They were in Ethiopia studying geladas, a kind of monkey, for a University of Pisa project called BRIDGES.

“It is a lovely reminder that careful field observation can reveal questions we had never thought to ask,” she said.

In a recent development, the pasture is in Debre Libanos, in Ethiopia’s Oromia region. Achille and Patroclo belonged to different owners. They met only during the day, when cattle and donkeys shared the pasture in mixed herds.

At night, Achille was housed with another adult bull, a cow, and a calf. Patroclo was housed with two other male donkeys.

Both animals had other possible partners in the same pasture. On any given day, there were three to six bulls and three to seven cows. There were also three male donkeys and two to seven female donkeys.

When the bull and the donkey kept interacting, Palagi noted, the team began documenting the pair systematically.

It has been revealed that the researchers recorded how Achille and Patroclo behaved toward each other and toward the rest of the herd. They kept recording even when nothing sexual was happening.

In all, the team saw the two together on four days and apart on four more.

Recent findings suggest that thirty-four of the 51 mounts included penetration. The researchers saw no avoidance and no aggression between the two animals.

It has been revealed that asked what surprised her most, Palagi named two things. One was how selective the two animals were about each other. The other was how actively Patroclo took part.

“What initially looked like an unusual encounter turned out to be a persistent pattern of preferential interaction,” Palagi told Earth.com.

Recent findings suggest that patroclo often presented his hindquarters to Achille and nipped him. Twice, another bull tried to come near Patroclo. Patroclo chased and bit him.

It has been revealed that the two animals also licked, rubbed, and nuzzled each other. The team looked closely at the six seconds or so around each mount.

Recent findings suggest that in about a quarter of the mounts, that friendly contact happened just before. In nearly three-quarters, it happened just after.

Contact before a mount isn’t a surprise, the authors wrote, because it may make mounting easier. Contact afterward is harder to explain. It appears to keep the social interaction going after sex is over.

Palagi said Achille and Patroclo had friendly contact with each other more often than with other animals, and it lasted longer.

The two also stayed close. When both were in the pasture, they spent more time near each other than apart.

Achille approached and mounted another male donkey only twice. That donkey avoided him and flattened its ears, a threatening expression.

According to recent reports, when Achille tried to mount the other donkey, Patroclo moved toward Achille. Achille immediately stopped and directed his friendly behavior at Patroclo instead.

According to recent reports, the researchers also analyzed Patroclo’s facial expressions using a coding system developed for horses. They compared four situations: Achille mounting him, Achille making friendly contact, Achille standing close by, and Patroclo alone.

Across all four, Patroclo’s face highlighted no detectable difference. To the team, that suggests Patroclo didn’t see Achille as a threat.

Achille courted cows the way bulls usually do, but he never tried to mount one. The other bulls nearby may have discouraged him, the researchers wrote.

After similar courtship with Patroclo, Achille did mount him.

The one time another bull tried to mount Achille, Achille rejected him. Among the rest of the herd, the team recorded no mounting between cattle and donkeys during the study.

Same-sex sexual behavior is widespread in animals. It has been documented in several species of the horse family.

But the team couldn’t find a published report of such behavior in donkeys. They also found no report of a lasting sexual relationship between domestic hoofed animals of two different species.

Classic explanations for same-sex sexual behavior include one animal forcing another, mistaken identity, and a shortage of opposite-sex partners.

The authors wrote that none of these seems to fully explain Achille and Patroclo. Their relationship was selective and mutual.

In a recent development, A bond like this must also come at a cost. The two spent time and energy on each other that could have gone into producing offspring. To the authors, the strength of the bond seems to outweigh that cost.

“Their relationship reminds us that sexual behavior can be part of a social bond beyond reproduction, and that these bonds can cross species boundaries,” Palagi mentioned.

According to recent reports, nobody knows yet what the bond does for either animal. The behavior may benefit one or both of them directly. Or it may be a result of the way cattle and donkeys form social bonds.

Palagi said the team can’t tell whether sex helped keep the bond going or came out of an attachment the two animals already had.

In a recent development, domestication may have played a part in the behavior too. The authors wrote that it changes animals’ social settings and their chances to interact with other species.

The next step, Palagi said, is to find out how often relationships like this one occur and to follow them over time.

In a recent development, she suggested comparing friendly behavior and signs of tension before and after sex. That could help test whether sex is linked to keeping a relationship going or to easing tension.

The team would also need to observe different pairs in different social settings to tell those two possibilities apart, she stated.

The full study was published in the journal Current Biology.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.

Grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” states Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”.

Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.

Moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.

According to recent reports, “My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz claims. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”.

Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (785 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21.
  • Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

He said “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the concerns were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”.

Recent findings suggest that earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from latest software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin noted “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”.

Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

Industry observers note that “This is an emergency,” he mentioned. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”.

The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

Mullin said the new $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

“We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin said. "Nickel and diming it together does not work.".

It has been revealed that thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications.".

Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment.".

Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

Sources indicate that the 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight aims. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

The committee’s majority said Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a upcoming one was built.

Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., stated in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications problems.

“Technology problems related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell mentioned.

Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and remarked their committee would “thoroughly review the challenges that led to this nationwide ground stop.”.

Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

Recent findings suggest that at issue in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have remarked they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

#157459. Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

📅 16 May 2025 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1637 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Godsavethepoints ↗ Open Full Page

Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

📅 16 May 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1637 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Godsavethepoints

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for Fresh York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots.
  • In a recent development, in 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies.
  • In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for Fresh York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In a recent development, in 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

Sources indicate that the whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic launched in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

Industry observers note that the fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following….

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter firm which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have….

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

It has been revealed that the truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

Industry observers note that on real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

According to recent reports, I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

According to recent reports, their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

Recent findings suggest that the app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

All the great, big airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

Recent findings suggest that and in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

According to recent reports, let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and company books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

Recent findings suggest that james Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so substantial time!

In a recent development, the business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

In a recent development, I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his firm ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

It has been revealed that my only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

Industry observers note that so yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or upcoming seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a new golden age, again.

Breaking: This scientist proves which problems computers can’t solve swiftly

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • In a recent development, dor Minzer remembers sitting in an undergraduate computation class at Tel Aviv University.
  • “My part is actually to prove not only do I not know how to do it, but I can prove that it’s impossible,” Minzer indicates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In a recent development, dor Minzer remembers sitting in an undergraduate computation class at Tel Aviv University. He was intrigued by his professor and soon found himself pulled into a new world: the mystifying intersection of math and computation, first laid out by Alan Turing during World War II. Working with the professor, Minzer became deeply interested in the limitations of what computers can and can’t do.

“My part is actually to prove not only do I not know how to do it, but I can prove that it’s impossible,” Minzer indicates. “You have to really be curious.”.

It has been revealed that minzer’s hard work has paid off. In 2018, he proved a theoretical computer science problem called the 2-to-2 games conjecture. It asks whether computers can efficiently distinguish games where almost all rules can be satisfied from those where almost none can be satisfied, when the rules have a strict structure.

Recent findings suggest that in September, Minzer and his two graduate students at MIT posted a 95-page milestone paper on the unique games conjecture, which builds off the 2-to-2 conjecture. The paper wasn’t quite ready, but they published to get ahead of a press release from OpenAI, describing its proof for the same problem, slated for only days later. It’s a situation that many mathematicians have found themselves in this year as AI companies flood the field with findings at lightning speed.

Minzer says it’s critical to remember that math, and all the research and contemplation behind it, is very human. “It’s a human activity,” he says. “Research is sort of a living organism, a living body.”.

Industry observers note that minzer teaches his own students now. Some days, he talks to his class and gets the sense that nobody is paying attention. But other days, he gets a few students that participate. They have ideas, they’re excited, and they remind him of his own days as a graduate student.

Sources indicate that “I feel like now I feel like I’m passing the torch,” he notes. “Before you have a Ph.D. adviser, you’re like a new person in a dark room. There are infinite places to go. Your Ph.D. adviser is the person that holds your hand and says, ‘Okay, let’s walk here.’”.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and new.

According to recent reports, to piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.

Industry observers note that most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo notes. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”.

In the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo says. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

Sources indicate that the lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December. The primary legislative business this week is the Senate's bipartisan permitting overhaul, but a late-breaking aviation funding fight and the Senate Democratic leadership contest are also commanding attention.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and both men are accumulating supporters ahead of leadership votes that are currently scheduled for early December — though there's been an effort to move that up to this week.

Van Hollen has expressed disagreement with Schumer's participation in primaries.

​"I don't think it's the role of the Senate majority leader to get involved in open, contested Democratic primaries," Van Hollen said Sunday on CNN.

​Van Hollen has also said he wants to use all available tools to stop funding for the Iran war immediately, with a government funding deadline in December. That's going to be one of several flash points for December's funding discussions, as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans try to use what leverage they have before Democrats take the gavels in the House and the Senate in January.

A fresh matter is the state of federal air traffic control after Friday's nationwide ground stop, with the Trump administration now seeking $50 billion to upgrade systems.

"I need additional money to do the additional work to keep the airspace safe," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Fox News Sunday.

Industry observers note that sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, a senior appropriator who is in line to become majority whip, has suggested reallocating funds from the additional money the Trump administration and congressional Republicans allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement to address the challenges at the Federal Aviation Administration.

Industry observers note that "There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars," Schatz posted on X.

Recent findings suggest that "We can do all things, we don't have to do one versus the other," Duffy noted in the Fox News Sunday interview. "I don't think that is the answer. The answer is let's do everything that's going to keep Americans safe, whether it's with immigration or it's with air travel.".

Sources indicate that meanwhile on the Senate floor, the energy permitting overhaul bill faces a key test Monday evening​, with a vote scheduled to limit debate on a substitute amendment that represents the most recent version of the bill. Votes on a number of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations are also lined up this week.

According to recent reports, on the other side of the Capitol, the House floor schedule i​ncludes several labor-related bills. ​One of the measures, introduced by Sen.-elect Kevin Hern, R-Okla.,​ would set standards for the way labor law applies to franchise operators.

New member orientation is also continuing, and committees in both the House and Senate will be holding hearings throughout the week as the outgoing Republican committee chairs aim to get through priority items on their agenda before the end of the Congress.

That includes a Tuesday morning Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, the nominee to be Navy secretary, who is currently the acting secretary. The Senate Judiciary Committee will be busy as well, as Chairman Charles E. Grassley, R-Iowa, looks to tee up more of Trump's judicial nominations for floor consideration.

The lowest star in that line is Alnitak (Zeta [ζ] Orionis), and the Orion Nebula lies just 3.7° south-southwest of this star, to its lower right on the sky this evening. In the brightest portion of the nebula lies a small grouping of young stars called the Trapezium Cluster. Take your time with this gorgeous sight, scanning around the region to pick out detail in the nebulosity. And if you are an astrophotographer, consider turning the view into a Thanksgiving memory to share for years to come.

Motion under the ocean explains the depth of the world’s deepest spot

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.
  • Now, scientists have a upcoming clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.

Now, scientists have a upcoming clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.

Challenger Deep is found within the Mariana Trench, a crescent-shaped gouge in the seafloor east of the Philippines in the Pacific Ocean. The trench is the scene of a slo-mo tectonic collision called a subduction zone: The Pacific plate is diving beneath the Mariana plate, bending downward as it sinks into the mantle, forming a steep trench on the ocean floor.

All subduction zones are deep, but “it’s interesting why this is the deepest spot in the Earth’s ocean,” says geoscientist Robert Stern, an emeritus professor at the University of Texas at Dallas and a visiting researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Recent findings suggest that he and colleagues employed a remotely operated robot called ROV Jason/Medea to descend to more than 6,000 meters and explore the Mariana Trench seafloor around the edges of Challenger Deep. The rocks turned out to contain pyroclastic deposits, evidence of an erstwhile explosive volcanic eruption. Those deposits included platelike blocks that could indicate eruption pulses, and lobe-shaped rocks where the volcanic flows ended and promptly cooled.

These are the deepest pyroclastic deposits found on Earth, the scientists report November 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science.

Recent findings suggest that how explosive an eruption is at Earth’s surface depends on the chemical makeup of the magma. When the molten rock contains a high proportion of volatile gases, including water vapor, those gases suddenly expand when the magma reaches the surface, producing a violent explosion.

According to recent reports, such explosive volcanism shouldn’t be possible in the deep sea; the pressure is too high for any escaping gases to expand, Stern states. Along with that mystery, the volcanic deposits were found unusually close to the trench, compared with what would be expected for a subduction zone.

Stern and his colleagues developed a hypothesis that incorporates these disparate pieces of evidence: The extreme depth of Challenger Deep, they say, may be at least partially due to an especially sharp bend in the Pacific Plate as it sinks into the mantle.

That tighter bend would explain why volcanism is happening closer to the subduction zone than usual. The classic subduction zone scenario is that the sinking plate heats up and melts partially as it descends; the magma rises through the overhanging plate and erupts, forming volcanic island arcs several hundred kilometers from the collision zone. Here, the volcanic deposits were just a hundred kilometers or so from the trench — which makes sense if the plate is dipping more steeply.

As for the pyroclastics, “we can’t answer if the eruptions were really explosive,” Stern indicates. But at those pressures, any gases such as water vapor contained in the magma wouldn’t be able to explosively expand as they would at the surface.

Instead, the pyroclastic rocks might have formed through a new version of deep-sea eruption, one in which water emerging from the magma is initially in a supercritical fluid state. That would minimize any explosive expansion during the eruption and could also produce fragmented, dense deposits like those seen by Jason/Medea.

The discovery of deep-sea pyroclastics is “surprising and unprecedented,” says William Chadwick, a geologist at Oregon State University in Newport. Challenger Deep may be the only place on Earth “with the ingredients to produce explosive volcanism in the super-deep ocean,” he says. “Imagining this happening is … pretty mind-boggling.”.

A lot more work remains to be done to evaluate all of these new ideas, Stern says. “But a lot of things are now coming together.”.
